Question: How do I stop worrying about the future?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The future will be met with the same reason that serves today. Leave it alone until it arrives, and give the present its full attention.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Worry is an attempt to live a day that has not arrived yet, with tools you will only have once you get there. Whatever comes, you will meet it with the same good sense you are using today. It's like driving at night: the headlights only show the next stretch of road, and that is enough to get you all the way home.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You will come to it, if need be, with the same power to reason, as you use upon your present business.

Question: Why do I feel anxious when nothing is actually wrong?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The trouble is rarely the thing itself. It is the judgement formed about it, and that judgement can be withdrawn at any moment.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Most anxiety comes from the story the mind tells about a situation, more than from the situation. A story is something you wrote, so you can put it down. It's like a smoke alarm going off over burnt toast: the noise is real, there is no fire, and you are allowed to press the button.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): When you are grieved about anything external it is not the thing itself which afflicts you, but your judgment about it. This judgment it is in your power to efface. If you are grieved about anything in your own disposition, who can prevent you from correcting your principles of life?

Question: How do I calm down when my mind is racing?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Blot out the imagination, check the impulse, and confine attention to the present moment. Calm returns quickly once a troubling thought is refused.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A racing mind is running several films at once. Stop the films, don't act on the first urge, and bring your attention back to the one thing in front of you. It's like a laptop slowed down by thirty open tabs: close them, keep one, and it runs smoothly again.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Blot out imagination. Check the brutal impulses of the passions. Confine your energies to the present time. Observe clearly all that happens either to yourself or to another.

Question: What should I do when I imagine the worst-case scenario?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Say no more to yourself than what the first appearance reports. "The child is ill" is the report. "The child is in danger" is an addition of one's own.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Separate what you actually know from what you have added. "The child has a fever" is a fact. "Something terrible is coming" is your own commentary. It's like a weather app that says rain is possible: that is the report. "The whole trip is ruined" is nowhere on the screen.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is told you that so-and-so has spoken ill of you. This alone is told you, and not that you are hurt by it. I see my child is sick; this only I see. I do not see that he is in danger.

Question: How do I stop overthinking everything?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Most troubles lie wholly in opinion and can be dropped. Clear them out and there is at once a wide space to move in.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Most of what is weighing on you exists only as opinion, and an opinion can be dropped. Drop the ones you don't need and you will find far more room than you expected. It's like a phone that says its storage is full: delete the blurry photos you will never look at, and it works fine again.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You can suppress many of the superfluous troubles which beset you, for they lie wholly in your own opinion. By this you will give ample room and ease to your life.

Question: I feel overwhelmed by everything that could go wrong. Where do I start?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not take in the whole of life at once. Ask only what in this present moment is unbearable, and the burden shrinks to its true size.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't try to carry your whole life at once. Ask one question: what, in this hour, is actually unbearable? Usually the answer is nothing. It's like a staircase: nobody can climb a whole flight in one stride, and anyone can take the next step.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Do not confound yourself by considering the whole of life, and by dwelling upon the multitude and greatness of the pains and troubles to which you may probably be exposed.

Question: How do I face something I am dreading?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Nothing can happen that a person is not fitted by nature to bear. Others have met the same and stood firm.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People are built to carry what life hands them, and plenty have faced this exact thing and stayed standing. You are made of the same material. It's like the first day at a new school or job: the dread in the car park was far worse than the day turned out to be.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Nothing can befall any man which he is not fitted by nature to bear. The like events befall others, and either through ignorance that the event has happened, or from ostentation of magnanimity, they stand firm and unhurt by them.

Question: How do I handle fear of public speaking?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Consider who the audience are and how little their approval finally matters. Then speak plainly and soundly, with dignity and without ornament.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at who is in the room and how much their approval will matter in a year. Then say what is true, plainly, without trying to dazzle. It's like giving directions to a lost driver: you don't perform. You tell them clearly where to go, and that is exactly what they need.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Speak, whether in the Senate or elsewhere, with dignity rather than elegance; and let your words ever be sound and virtuous.

Question: How do I stop being afraid of what people think?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look closely at the people whose opinion is feared: what they pursue, what they flee, and how they judge themselves. The fear fades on inspection.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Study the people whose judgement scares you: what they chase, what they run from, how harshly they judge themselves. Up close, their verdict loses its power. It's like the audience at a talent show: once you see how quickly they cheer and boo the same act, their verdict stops feeling like the truth.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Penetrate the souls of men, and you will see what judges you fear, and how they sit in judgment on themselves.

Question: I am afraid of change. How should I think about it?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Nothing comes into being without change. Food cannot nourish and wood cannot warm unless it changes. One's own change is of the same kind, and as needful to nature.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Nothing good exists without change. Food has to change to feed you, and wood has to burn to warm you. Your own change is the same process. It's like a phone update: the screen looks unfamiliar for a day, and nothing could ever improve if the software stayed frozen.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Observe continually that all things exist in change; and keep this thought ever with you, that Nature loves nothing more than changing what things now are, and making others like them.

Question: How do I cope with uncertainty about my job or income?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Attend to what is in one's power: the next right act, done well. What lies outside one's power is neither good nor evil in itself.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Put your effort into the part that is yours: the next piece of work, done well. Whether the company keeps you or the market turns is outside your hands, and it is neither good nor bad until you decide what to do with it. It's like sailing: nobody can order the wind, and anyone can trim the sail.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whenever we imagine that anything which lies not in our power is good or evil for us, if the evil befall us or if we miss the good, we inevitably blame the Gods, and hate the men who are, or whom we suspect to be, the cause of our disaster or our loss.

Question: How do I stop fearing failure?
Marcus Aurelius would say: When an act is blocked, the mind turns the block into material for another act. Every hindrance to the work becomes help.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: When one route is blocked, the mind can use the block itself as material for the next move. A setback is raw material. It's like a navigation app when a road is closed: it does not shut down and call the trip a failure. It says "rerouting" and finds another way.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): For the mind can convert and change everything that impedes its activity into matter for its action; hindrance in its work becomes its real help, and every obstruction makes for its progress.

Question: Is it normal to be afraid of dying?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Fear of death is fear either of feeling nothing or of feeling something new. If nothing, there is no harm to feel. If something new, life goes on in another form.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes, it is normal. But look at what the fear is of: either you will feel nothing, so there is nothing to suffer, or you will experience something new, so life continues in another form. It's like falling asleep each night: you lose awareness completely, and it has never once hurt you.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He who dreads death dreads either the extinction of all sense or the experience of a new one. If all sense be extinguished, there can be no sense of evil. If a different sort of sense be acquired you become a different creature, and do not cease to live.

Question: How do I deal with panic in the moment?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Return to yourself quickly, and do not stay out of tune longer than the moment forces. Mastery of the inner harmony grows by coming back to it again and again.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Panic knocks you out of tune. The job is to get back in tune quickly, not to never be knocked. The more often you return, the faster it gets. It's like a musician whose string slips mid-song: they don't stop the concert. They retune and carry on, and with practice it takes seconds.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whenever your situation forces trouble upon you, return quickly to yourself, and interrupt the rhythm of life no longer than you are compelled. Your grasp of the harmony will grow surer by continual recurrence to it.

Question: I worry constantly about my children's safety. What would he say?
Marcus Aurelius would say: A healthy eye looks at everything visible and does not demand only green. A healthy mind is ready for whatever happens, and does not plead "let my children be spared".
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A healthy mind is ready for whatever happens. It doesn't bargain with life for a guarantee, because no parent has ever been given one. It's like an experienced sailor: they check the forecast and still prepare for every kind of weather, because the sea never promised calm.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The healthy eye ought to look on everything visible, and not to say, “I want green,” like an eye that is diseased. Sound hearing or sense of smell ought to be ready for all that can be heard or smelt; and the healthy stomach should be equally disposed for all sorts of food, as a mill for all that it was built to grind.

Question: How do I stop my imagination running away with me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Speak to it directly: be gone as you came, there is no need of you. Imagination arrives by old habit and can be dismissed without anger.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: An anxious picture shows up out of old habit, and its arrival is no proof that it is true. You can speak to it calmly: you came uninvited, and you can leave. It's like a pop-up ad: it appears by itself, you don't have to read it, and you certainly don't have to click.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be gone, I say, even as you came. I have no need for you. You came, you say, after your ancient fashion: I am not angry with you, only, be gone!

Question: What can I do about worries that keep me up at night?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It was a dream that troubled you. Wake, come back to your senses, and look at these things as you looked at those.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What troubles you at three in the morning is closer to a bad dream than to a fact. Wake up properly, and look at your worries in daylight the way you look at a dream. It's like a coat on a chair that looks like an intruder in the dark: switch on the light and it is a coat.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Shake sleep from you, and know that it was a dream that troubled you; and, now that you are broad awake again, regard the waking world as you did the dream.

Question: How do I find safety when the world feels dangerous?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The mind that gathers into itself and refuses to do what it does not choose is a fortress. There is no safer refuge.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No outside place can be made perfectly safe, but your own mind can. When it decides what it will and will not go along with, nothing can break in. It's like a house in a storm: you can't stop the weather, you can close the door, and inside it stays dry.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember that the governing part becomes invincible when, collected into itself, it is satisfied in refusing to do what it would not, even when its resistance is unreasonable.

Question: Why do small things frighten me so much?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Much popular fear is a mask made to frighten children. Strip the thing bare, see what it is in itself, and it loses its terror.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Fear grows on things you haven't looked at properly. Strip the thing down, see what it is actually made of, and most of the terror falls off. It's like a haunted house ride with the lights switched on: plywood, paint and a loudspeaker.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Socrates called the maxims of the vulgar hobgoblins, bogies to frighten children.

Question: How do I build courage?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Live as a wrestler does: always on guard and firm against sudden attacks. Courage is practised by meeting what comes without being thrown.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Courage is a stance you practise, by staying on your feet each time life pushes. It is no use waiting to feel brave first. It's like training with weights: nobody gets strong by reading about it. You lift something slightly heavy, often, and one day the heavy thing isn't heavy.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The art of Life is more like that of the wrestler than of the dancer; for the wrestler must always be ready on his guard, and stand firm against the sudden, unforeseen efforts of his adversary.

Question: I have too much to do. How do I cope?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do what is necessary and what reason requires, and no more. Most of what is said and done is not necessary, and dropping it brings leisure and calm.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Most of what fills a day doesn't need doing. Do what is necessary, do it well, and drop the rest. The calm comes from the dropping. It's like packing for a flight with cabin luggage only: when the bag is small, you discover how little you needed to bring.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): This is perhaps a better saying, “Do what is necessary, do what the reason of the being that is social in its nature directs, and do it in the spirit of that direction.” By this you will attain the calm that comes from virtuous action, and that calm also which comes from having few things to do.

Question: How do I stay calm under pressure?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Be like the headland on which the waves keep breaking. It stands firm, and the swell of the water falls quiet around it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Pressure will keep coming, the way waves do. Your part is to stay put and let it break around you. It's like an experienced air traffic controller on a busy afternoon: the planes keep arriving, the voice stays level, and each one is handled in turn.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be like a promontory against which the waves are always breaking. It stands fast, and stills the waters that rage around it. “Wretched am I,” says one, “that this has befallen me.”

Question: How do I get through a really hard day?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Take the work one act at a time, as one would spell out a name letter by letter. Each duty has a number of parts; complete them in order, without fuss.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A hard day is a row of single tasks. Take them in order, one at a time, without drama. It's like a checkout worker facing a long queue: they serve the person in front of them, and the queue takes care of itself.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Should some one ask you how the name Antoninus is written, would you not carefully pronounce to him each one of the letters? Should he then begin an angry dispute about it, would you also grow angry, and not rather mildly count over the several letters to him?

Question: I feel burned out. What would he tell me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Withdraw into yourself for a short while. A few brief principles, recalled there, are enough to wash away the weariness and send one back without resentment.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You don't need two weeks away. You need a few minutes alone with the handful of ideas that steady you, and then you go back without resentment. It's like plugging a phone in for ten minutes: it isn't a full charge, it is enough to get you through, and you can do it anywhere.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Have also at hand thoughts brief and fundamental, which readily may occur; sufficing to shut out the discordant clamour of the world, and to send you back without fretting at the task to which you return.

Question: How do I stop feeling like everything is urgent?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Before all things, do not be disturbed. Everything follows the nature of the whole, and in a little while this too will be gone.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Very little is truly urgent. Things take their course, and most of today's emergencies will be forgotten shortly. It's like an inbox where every email is marked high priority: when everything carries the red flag, the flag means nothing, and you are free to decide what comes first.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Everything comes to pass as directed by universal Nature, and in a little time you will be departed and gone, like Hadrianus and Augustus. Then, scan closely the nature of what has befallen, remembering that it is your duty to be a good man.

Question: How do I cope when life feels chaotic?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Whether the world is order or confusion, one's own part is the same: keep the ruling mind steady. If the wave sweeps something off, let it be the body and never the mind.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Whether the world is orderly or a mess, your job is the same: keep your own mind steady. If something has to get knocked about, let it be your plans or your comfort, never your judgement. It's like a pilot in turbulence: the cabin shakes, and the hands on the controls don't.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): There is either a fatal necessity, an unalterable order, or a placable Providence, or a blind confusion without a governor. If there be an unalterable necessity, why strive against it?

Question: I can't switch off from work. What should I do?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Rest is found within, at any hour, by retiring into one's own mind. Go there often and briefly, and return to the work renewed.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Rest isn't somewhere you travel to. It is a place inside your own head that you can step into for a minute at any hour, and then return. It's like the airplane mode switch: the phone is still in your hand, the work is still there, and for a short while nothing gets through.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Nowhere can a man find any retreat more quiet and more full of leisure than in his own soul; especially when there is that within it on which, if he but look, he is straightway quite at rest.

Question: How do I deal with constant interruptions?
Marcus Aurelius would say: When outside things distract, make time to learn something good and stop being whirled around. Guard also against the other error: busyness with no aim.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: When outside noise keeps pulling at you, turn deliberately to something worth learning, so you stop spinning. Watch for the opposite mistake too: being busy with no aim. It's like a dog chasing every car that passes: a lot of running, and no destination.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Cares from without distract you: take leisure, then, to add some good thing to your knowledge; have done with vacillation, and avoid the other error. For triflers, too, are they who, by their activities, weary themselves in life, and have no settled aim to which they may direct, once and for all, their every desire and project.

Question: How do I stop taking on too much?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask of each thing: is this one of the necessary ones? The question applies to thoughts as well as acts, since needless thoughts lead to needless acts.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Before saying yes, ask one question: is this one of the necessary things? Ask it of your thoughts as well, because unnecessary thoughts turn into unnecessary commitments. It's like a doorman with a guest list: if the name isn't on it, it doesn't come in, however nicely it asks.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): On every occasion, then, ask yourself the question, Is this thing not unnecessary? And put away not only unnecessary deeds but unnecessary thoughts, for by so doing you will avoid all superfluous actions.

Question: How do I handle a crisis at work?
Marcus Aurelius would say: First ask whether one's own understanding is equal to it. If it is, use it. If it is not, hand the work to someone better able, or do it with their help.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: First ask plainly whether you have the skill for this. If you do, use it. If you don't, hand it to someone who does, or work alongside them. It's like a family doctor referring you to a specialist: that is good medicine, and nobody calls it failure.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If it be sufficient, I use it for the work in hand as an instrument given to me by nature. If it be not sufficient, I either give place to one better fitted for the achievement, or, if for some reason this be not a proper course, I do it as best I can, taking the aid of those who, by directing my mind, can accomplish something fit and serviceable for the common good.

Question: How do I stop complaining about my situation?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Is the gourd bitter? Put it down. Are there thorns in the path? Step aside. That is enough, without adding "why do such things exist?"
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Deal with the thing and skip the commentary. If something is unpleasant, put it down or go round it. Asking why such things exist adds nothing. It's like hitting a pothole: you steer round the next one. You don't park the car and give a speech about potholes.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Is the gourd bitter? Put it from you. Are there thorns in the way? Walk aside. That is enough. Do not add, “Why were such things brought into the world?” The naturalist would laugh at you, just as would a carpenter or a shoemaker, if you began fault-finding because you saw shavings and parings from their work strewn about the workshop.

Question: Everything is going wrong at once. How should I see it?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Not "how unlucky that this has happened to me", but "how fortunate that I can bear it without being crushed". Dwell on the strength, not on the mishap.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Change the sentence you are saying to yourself. Not "how unlucky I am", but "how good that I can take this and still be standing". Put the attention on your strength. It's like a phone that survives a drop on the pavement: you don't mourn the fall. You are glad it was built well.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Why, then, should we dwell more on the misfortune of the incident than on the felicity of such strength of mind? Can you call that a misfortune for a man which is not a miscarriage of his nature?

Question: How do I keep perspective when I'm stressed?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look at it from above: herds, armies, weddings, births, deaths, the noise of the courts. Then consider how many have never heard your name.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Zoom out. See the whole busy world at once, people being born, getting married, arguing in court, and notice how few of them have ever heard your name. It's like a satellite map zoomed all the way out: the traffic jam you were stuck in is no longer even a line.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): on all things earthly; on herds and armies; on husbandry and marriage; on partings, births, and deaths; on the tumults of the courts of justice; on the desert places of the earth; on the varied spectacle of savage nations; on feasting and lamentation; on traffic; on the medley of all things, and the order which emerges from their contrariety.

Question: How do I stop bringing stress home?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Whatever the situation forced on you, come back to yourself quickly. Do not carry the discord further than the moment required.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Whatever the day forced on you, come back to yourself quickly once it is over. Don't carry the bad mood one step further than it had to go. It's like muddy boots: you take them off at the door, because the mud belongs to the field and not to the living room.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whenever your situation forces trouble upon you, return quickly to yourself, and interrupt the rhythm of life no longer than you are compelled. Your grasp of the harmony will grow surer by continual recurrence to it.

Question: What is the quickest way to feel calm?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is easy to push away every disturbing impression and be at once in perfect calm. The power to do so is always at hand.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Calm is closer than it feels. You can refuse an upsetting thought the moment it arrives and be steady at once. It's like the mute button on a remote: the noise seems to fill the room, one press ends it, and the remote was in your hand the whole time.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How easy it is to thrust away and blot out each impression that is disturbing and unfit; and forthwith to enjoy perfect tranquillity.

Question: How do I deal with pressure from other people's expectations?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Much leisure is gained by not looking at what a neighbour says or does or intends, and looking only at what one does oneself, that it be just.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You free up a great deal of time and energy when you stop watching what other people say, do and expect, and attend only to whether your own actions are right. It's like a runner in a race: every glance at the other lanes costs speed. Run your own lane.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How much he gains in leisure who looks not to what his neighbours say, or do, or intend; but considers only how his own actions may be just and holy, looking not, as Agathon says, to the moral example of others, but running a straight course and never turning therefrom.

Question: I feel like I'm failing at everything. What now?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not fret or lose heart if not every act goes by principle. When thrown off, come back again, and be glad if most of what is done is worthy of a human being.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Not every day will go by your principles. When you slip, come back, and count it a win if most of what you do is decent. It's like a learner driver who stalls at a junction: you restart the engine and pull away again. You don't hand back the keys.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Fret not, neither despond nor be disheartened, if it be not always possible for you to act according to your principles of perfection. If you are beaten off, return again to the effort, and content yourself that your conduct is generally such as becomes a man.

Question: How do I find rest without going on holiday?
Marcus Aurelius would say: People seek retreats in the country, by the sea, in the hills. Nowhere is quieter or freer from trouble than one's own mind, and it is open at any hour.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The quiet you are looking for in the mountains or by the sea is available inside your own head, at any hour, for free. Go there briefly and often. It's like carrying noise-cancelling headphones: you can't silence the train, and you can still find quiet in the middle of it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Men seek retirement in the country, on the sea-coast, in the mountains; and you too have frequent longings for such distractions. Yet surely this is great folly, since you may retire into yourself at any hour you please.

Question: How do I stop dreading Mondays?
Marcus Aurelius would say: On waking unwillingly, keep this thought ready: I am rising to do the work of a human being. Was I made to lie under the blankets and keep warm?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: When you don't want to get up, remind yourself what you are getting up for: to do the work a human being is here to do. You weren't made to stay warm under a duvet. It's like a striker on match day: the bed is comfortable, and the bed is not where the game is played.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Am I equipped for nothing but to lie among the bed-clothes and keep warm? “But,” you say, “it is more pleasant so”. Is pleasure, then, the object of your being, and not action, and the exercise of your powers?

Question: How do I carry heavy responsibility without breaking?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Bear the work without acting the wretch, and without wanting pity or admiration. Want one thing only: to act or refrain as the common good requires.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Carry it without making yourself the suffering hero, and without fishing for sympathy or applause. Want one thing: to do what is good for the people who depend on you. It's like a good bus driver: a full bus behind them, no announcements about how hard it is, and a safe arrival.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Bear toil and pain, not as if wretched under it, nor as courting pity or admiration. Wish for one thing only; always to act or to refrain as social wisdom requires.

Question: How do I control my temper?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Keep ready the thought that gentleness is the stronger and more human quality. The calm person, and not the angry one, has strength, nerve and courage.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Gentleness is the stronger position. The person who stays calm is the one with real strength and nerve, and the one who explodes has lost control. It's like a martial arts black belt: the more skilled the fighter, the calmer they are, because they have nothing to prove.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Strength and nerves and courage are the portion of the meek and gentle man; and not of the irascible and impatient. For the nearer a man attains to freedom from passion, the nearer he comes to strength.

Question: Why do I get so angry at people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The anger comes from one's own opinion of the act, and not from the act. Take away the judgement that it is terrible, and the anger goes with it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What makes you angry is your reading of what they did, more than the act. Remove the verdict "this is outrageous" and the anger has nothing to stand on. It's like a text message with no emoji: the words are neutral, and the tone you hear in them is the one you supplied.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Thirdly: If they act rightly, we ought not to take it amiss; and, if not rightly, manifestly they do so without intention and in ignorance. For no soul is willingly deprived of truth, or of the faculty of treating every man as he deserves.

Question: What should I remember before I lose my temper?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Run through this: we were made for each other; they act from ignorance; you too do wrong; you cannot be sure of their motive; life is short.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Run through a short checklist: we are here to work together; they are acting out of ignorance; you get things wrong too; you can't be sure why they did it; and life is short. It's like a pilot's checklist before take-off: half a minute of routine that prevents the crash.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Fifthly: You cannot even be perfectly sure that wrong has been done, for many things admit of justification. And, generally speaking, a man must have learned much before he can pronounce surely upon the conduct of others.

Question: How do I deal with someone who keeps provoking me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Meekness is invincible when it is genuine. What can the most insolent person do if you stay gentle and, at the very moment, quietly set them right?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Real kindness can't be beaten. If you stay gentle and calmly point out the mistake at the very moment they are trying to wind you up, they have nothing to push against. It's like a tug of war: when you let go of the rope, the person pulling hardest is the one who falls over.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Ninthly: Meekness is invincible if it be genuine, without simper or hypocrisy. For what can the most insolent of men do to you, if you persist in civility towards him; and, if occasion offers, admonish him gently and deliberately, shew him the better way at the very moment that he is endeavouring to harm you?

Question: Is anger ever useful?
Marcus Aurelius would say: An angry face is against nature. Worn often, it kills the beauty of the countenance until it cannot be revived. Anger harms the angry person first.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Rarely. Anger damages the angry person first. Wear a scowl often enough and it settles into the face for good. It's like revving a car in neutral: a lot of noise and heat, the engine wears out, and the car hasn't moved.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): When the countenance is often thus deformed, its beauty dies, in the end is quenched for ever, and cannot be revived again. Seek to comprehend from this very fact that it is against reason.

Question: How do I stop holding grudges?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The best revenge is not to copy the one who did the wrong.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The best answer to someone who wronged you is not to become like them. A grudge keeps you tied to their behaviour. It's like paying rent on a flat you moved out of years ago: the only person it costs is you.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The best revenge is not to copy him that wronged you.

Question: How do I respond when someone insults me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Does someone despise me? That is their affair. Mine is to be found doing or saying nothing that deserves contempt, and to stay kind even to them.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If someone looks down on you, that is their business. Yours is to make sure you do nothing that deserves it, and to stay decent even toward them. It's like a referee being booed: the job is to call the game fairly, and the noise from the stands doesn't change a single rule.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): And let me look to it that I be found doing or saying nothing worthy of his contempt. Does any one hate me? That is his affair. I shall be kind and good-natured to every one, and ready to shew his mistake to him that hates me; not in order to upbraid him, or to make a show of my patience, but from genuine goodness, like Phocion, if he indeed was sincere.

Question: How do I stay calm when someone is rude?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Begin the day expecting to meet the meddling, the ungrateful and the insolent. They are so through ignorance of good and evil, and none of them can harm you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Start the day expecting to meet rude people. They behave that way because they haven't worked out what matters, and they can't damage your character. It's like roadworks on a route you drive every day: annoying, expected, and nothing personal.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Say this to yourself in the morning: Today I shall have to do with meddlers, with the ungrateful, with the insolent, with the crafty, with the envious and the selfish. All these vices have beset them, because they know not what is good and what is evil.

Question: I snapped at someone I love. What now?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Turn at once to your own fault and consider how you err in the same way. Then return to your principles without despair.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at your own fault first, without excuses, and remember that you do the very thing that annoys you in others. Then go back to your principles and repair it. It's like spilling coffee on a friend's table: you don't stand there in despair. You apologise, grab a cloth and clean it up.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): When you are offended at any one's fault, turn at once to yourself and consider of what similar fault you yourself are guilty; such as esteeming for good things, money, pleasure, a little glory, or the like.

Question: How do I stop getting angry at strangers, in traffic or in queues?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Are you angry at someone whose breath is foul? What is the use? People act from what they are. Reason with them if you can, or let it pass.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People act from what they are, and a stranger's slowness is no more aimed at you than bad breath would be. Help if you can, otherwise let it pass. It's like shouting at a red light: it changes at its own pace whether you fume or not.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Are you angry with one whose armpits smell or whose breath is foul? What is the use? His mouth or his arm-pits are so, and the consequence must follow. But, you say, man is a reasonable being, and could by attention discern in what he offends.

Question: How should I handle anger at injustice?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The wrongdoer wrongs himself, by making himself bad. Teach him better if you can. If you cannot, remember that patience was given you for exactly this.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The person who does wrong damages himself first, by becoming someone worse. Correct him if you can. If you can't, this is exactly what patience is for. It's like a good teacher with a pupil who cheats: the aim is to fix the behaviour, and the teacher's rage would add nothing to the lesson.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The wrong-doer wrongs himself by making himself evil.

Question: How do I avoid saying things I regret when angry?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask of every act: what is the effect of this for me, and shall I repent of it? A little while and all is over.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Before you speak or act, ask two questions: what will this do to me, and will I regret it? Give it a moment. It's like the "undo send" delay on an email: a few seconds' pause has saved a great many people from a message they could never take back.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Upon every action ask yourself, what is the effect of this for me? Shall I never repent of it? I shall presently be dead, and all these things gone. What more should I desire if my present action is becoming to an intelligent and a social being, subject to the same law with Gods?

Question: Why does anger feel so powerful?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It only seems strong. As grief is a weakness, so is anger: in both a person has been wounded and has given way.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Anger looks like power, and it is really a sign of being hurt. The angry person, like the grieving one, has taken a wound and buckled under it. It's like a car alarm: very loud, and what it tells you is that something got to the car, not that the car is strong.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): A weak man in grief is like a weak man in anger. Both are hurt, and both give way. If you want a tenth gift, from the Leader of the Muses, take this:— To expect the wicked not to sin is madness.

Question: How do I stop being irritated by people's habits?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is as foolish to be surprised that the world produces what it is bound to produce as to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People behave according to what they are, so being surprised by it is your mistake. It's like being annoyed that the sea is salty: that is what it is. Adjust around it, and save your surprise for something new.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember that, as 'tis folly to be surprised that a fig-tree bears figs, so is it equal folly to be surprised that the Universe produces those things of which it was ever fruitful.

Question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: When someone offends you, ask what notion of good or evil led them to it. Seeing that, you will pity them, and neither wonder nor be angry.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask what the person believed was good or bad when they did it. Once you see the mistaken idea they were acting on, pity takes the place of anger. It's like someone who gives you wrong directions because their map is out of date: the harm was real, and they were lost too.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): When you see where his error lies you will pity him, and be neither surprised nor angry. Indeed you yourself perhaps still wrongly count good the same things as he does, or things just like them.

Question: What if the person does not deserve forgiveness?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The gods, who live forever, bear with the wicked through endless time, and even care for them. Will you, who are so soon to die, grow tired of it?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Deserving has little to do with it. Life puts up with people's failings endlessly, and you are asked to manage it only for a short time. It's like the sun, which shines on every house in the street without first checking who has earned it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The Gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that in a long eternity they must ever bear with the wickedness and the multitude of sinners. Nay, they even lavish on them all manner of loving care.

Question: How do I stop reacting instantly?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Wipe out the impression, stay the impulse, quench the desire. Keep the governing part master of itself.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Put a gap between the trigger and the response: drop the picture, hold the impulse, cool the want. Let the thinking part stay in charge. It's like a hot pan on the stove: you don't grab it the instant you see it. You pause, reach for a cloth, and then pick it up.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Wipe out impression; stay impulse; quench desire; and keep the governing part master of itself.

Question: How do I stay gentle and still be firm?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Be gentle with those who obstruct you and steady in your own course. To grow angry with them is as weak as to give up and submit.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be kind to the people in your way and unmoved about your direction. Losing your temper and giving in are the same weakness in two forms. It's like a good nurse with a patient who refuses the medicine: a warm voice, a steady hand, and the medicine still gets taken.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is equally weak to grow angry with them or to desist from action and submit to defeat. Both are equally deserters— he who runs away, and he who refuses to stand by friend and kinsman.

Question: How do I deal with anger at myself?
Marcus Aurelius would say: "I have no right to vex myself, who never yet willingly vexed anyone." Correct the fault and go on.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You wouldn't deliberately torment anyone else, so you have no right to torment yourself. Fix the fault and move on. It's like a coach with a player who misses: a good coach corrects the technique and sends them back on. Screaming at the player only makes the next shot worse.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I have no right to vex myself who never yet willingly vexed any one.

Question: How do I teach myself patience?
Marcus Aurelius would say: People were made for one another: teach them better, or bear with them. Recall also how much you have already borne.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Remember that people are here for each other: either help them do better or put up with them. And remember how much you have already managed to put up with. It's like teaching a child to tie shoelaces: it takes far longer than doing it yourself, and the waiting is the teaching.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Teach them better then, or bear with them.

Question: I feel low for no clear reason. What would he advise?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look within. Inside is the spring of good, and it keeps flowing if you keep digging. If the low mood lasts, speak to a doctor as well.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look inward before looking for a fix outside. There is a source of good in you that keeps giving if you keep going back to it. It's like a well in a dry season: the water is still there, and it takes more digging. If the low mood stays, see a doctor as well, as you would for a pain that won't go.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Within is the fountain of Good. Dig constantly and it will ever well forth.

Question: How do I cheer myself up?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Think of the good qualities of those around you: this one's energy, that one's modesty, another's generosity. Nothing cheers so much as virtues seen in the people one lives with.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Think about what is good in the people around you: one person's energy, another's modesty, another's generosity. Nothing lifts the mood faster. It's like scrolling back through old photos of friends: within a minute you are smiling, and nothing in your day has changed except where you looked.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Nothing rejoices the heart so much as instances, the more the better, of goodness manifested in the characters of those around us. Let us, therefore, have such instances ever present for reflection.

Question: How do I stop feeling sorry for myself?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Picture everyone who grieves or storms at anything as the pig that kicks and squeals at the sacrifice. Only the reasoning creature can follow willingly.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Kicking and wailing against what happens changes nothing except how you go through it. You have something better: the ability to accept it and walk forward. It's like a child being carried out of a toy shop: the leaving happens either way. The only choice is whether you walk out on your own feet.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Imagine every one who is grieved or storms about anything whatever, to be like the pig in a sacrifice, which kicks and screams under the knife. Such, too, is he who, on his couch, deplores in silence, by himself, that we are all tied to our fate.

Question: I feel alone. What would he say?
Marcus Aurelius would say: A branch cut from its neighbour is cut from the whole tree. A person severs himself by turning away, and it lies in his power to grow together again.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Loneliness often starts with pulling away. When you cut yourself off from the people near you, you cut yourself off from everyone, and you are also the one who can reconnect. It's like a phone left in airplane mode: the network never went anywhere. You switch it back on.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): A branch cut off from its adjacent branch must necessarily be severed from the whole tree. Even so a man, parted from any fellow-man, has fallen away from the whole social community.

Question: How do I cope with loneliness?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You are a limb of the one body of reasoning beings, and not merely a part of it. Act from that, and kindness becomes a delight and not only a duty.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You aren't a spare part sitting next to humanity. You are a working part of it, the way a hand is part of a body. Act from that, and being kind stops being a chore and becomes a pleasure. It's like playing in a band: the bass player isn't lonely, because the song needs the bass.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In an organic unity bodily members play the same part as reasoning beings among separate existences, since both are fitted for one joint operation. This thought will come home to you the more vividly if you say often to yourself: “I am a member of the mighty organism which is made up of reasoning beings.”

Question: How can I be content on my own?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Retire within. The reasoning mind is by nature content with itself when it acts justly, and so finds calm.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Go inward. A mind that knows it is acting fairly is good company for itself, and that brings a calm no one else has to supply. It's like someone who can eat alone in a restaurant and enjoy the meal: the table isn't empty, because they brought themselves.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The reasoning power that rules you naturally finds contentment with itself in just dealing, and in the calm which such dealing brings.

Question: How do I find joy in ordinary life?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Notice the charm in what comes of nature's work: the cracks in a baked loaf, ripe figs splitting open, the bend of heavy ears of corn.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Train your eye on the small things nature does without trying: the crack in a loaf of bread, a ripe fig splitting, wheat bending under its own weight. It's like using the camera on your phone: the moment you look for a good picture, you start finding one in an ordinary street.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Observe what grace and charm appear even in the accidents that accompany Nature's work. Thus some parts of a loaf crack and burst in the baking; and this cracking, though in a manner contrary to the design of the baker, looks well and invites the appetite.

Question: Why am I never satisfied?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Dwell less on what is lacking and more on what is present. Choose the best of what you have, and consider how you would long for it if it were gone.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You are looking at the gap and ignoring what is already there. Pick the best of what you have, and imagine how badly you would want it back if it were gone. It's like your own home after a long trip: nothing in it has changed, and your own bed suddenly feels like a luxury.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Select the best of what you have, and consider how passionately you would have longed for it had it not been yours. Yet be watchful, lest by this joy in what you have you accustom yourself to value it too highly; so that, if it should fail, you would be distressed.

Question: How do I stop comparing my life with other people's?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He is a better wrestler than you. But not more public-spirited, more modest, or better prepared for what happens.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Someone will always beat you at something. Nobody can stop you from being more generous, more modest or better prepared for what life brings, and those are the scores that count. It's like judging a doctor by how fast they can run: you are measuring the wrong thing.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He is a better wrestler than you, but not more public-spirited, more modest, or better prepared for the accidents of fate; not more gentle toward the short-comings of his neighbours.

Question: What actually makes a person happy?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Good fortune is a good spirit within. A happy life needs very little: to be free, modest, kind and obedient to what is right.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Happiness is a good state of mind, and it needs very little: to be free, modest, kind and to do what is right. It's like a good cup of tea: a few plain ingredients, done properly. Adding ten more things doesn't make it better.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To have good fortune is to have a good spirit, or a good mind. What do you here, Imagination? Be gone, I say, even as you came. I have no need for you. You came, you say, after your ancient fashion: I am not angry with you, only, be gone!

Question: I feel empty even though my life looks fine. Why?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You have tried many roads and found the good life in none: not in argument, wealth, fame or pleasure. It lies in doing what human nature requires.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You have tried the usual roads, clever arguments, money, reputation, pleasure, and none of them delivered. The good life is in doing what a human being is built for: thinking well and being useful to others. It's like filling a car with the wrong fuel: the tank reads full, and the engine still won't run.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You have made many efforts and wandered much, but you have nowhere found happiness; not in syllogisms, not in riches, not in fame or pleasure, not in anything. Where, then, is it?

Question: How do I stop dwelling on the past?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let the past go, entrust the future to providence, and direct only the present toward reverence and justice.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Let the past go, leave the future to take care of itself, and put the present to good use. That is the only part you can touch. It's like driving while staring at the rear-view mirror: a glance is useful, and the road you can steer on is through the windscreen.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): That is to say, if you will leave behind you all that is past, commit the future to Providence, and regulate the present in piety and justice. In piety that you may love your appointed lot; for Nature gave it to you and you to it.

Question: How do I deal with boredom and sameness?
Marcus Aurelius would say: All of life repeats itself, like the shows at the amphitheatre. Take delight in one thing instead: passing from one unselfish act to the next.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Life does repeat. The same shows come round again. So stop waiting for novelty to rescue you, and take pleasure in something that never gets old: going from one useful, unselfish act to the next. It's like a baker: the same bread every morning, and a different person fed each time.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Find your sole delight and recreation in proceeding from one unselfish action to another, with God ever in mind.

Question: I feel like nobody understands me.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Enter into the governing mind of others, and let others enter into yours. Understanding begins by offering it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Understanding has to be offered before it is received. Make the effort to get inside other people's thinking, and let them into yours. It's like a handshake: someone has to reach out first.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Penetrate into the governing part of others; and also allow others to enter into your own.

Question: How do I keep going when I see no point?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not tire of receiving good by doing it; acting according to nature is one's own gain. If this feeling stays, tell someone you trust and see a doctor.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Keep doing small, good things for others even when you can't feel the point, because the doing is itself the gain. It's like walking in fog: you can't see the destination, and each step still carries you forward. If this feeling stays, tell someone you trust and see a doctor. Fog is easier with a guide.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): No man wearies of what brings him gain, and your gain lies in acting according to nature. Be not weary, therefore, of gaining by the act which gives others gain.

Question: How do I stop feeling like a victim?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Suppress the thought "I am hurt" and the hurt is gone.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Being hurt has two parts: what happened, and the sentence "I have been wronged" that you add. Take away the sentence and most of the hurt goes with it. It's like a foul in football: it lasts a second, and the player who stays down long after the whistle is the one who misses the rest of the game.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Suppress the thought; and the cry “I am hurt!” is gone. Suppress “I am hurt!” and you suppress the injury.

Question: Why do I feel worse after scrolling through other people's lives?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not waste what remains of life on thoughts about others, wondering what they do and why. It pulls the mind from its own work.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Time spent wondering what other people are doing, and why, is time taken from your own life and work. It's like standing in your kitchen watching the neighbours' dinner party through the window while your own food burns on the stove.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Waste not what remains of life in consideration about others, when it makes not for the common good. Be sure you are neglecting other work if you busy yourself with what such a one is doing and why, with what he is saying, thinking, or scheming.

Question: How do I find beauty when everything looks grey?
Marcus Aurelius would say: To one with feeling and insight into nature, hardly anything fails to please: even the jaws of wild beasts, and the ripeness of old age.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: To someone who looks with real attention, almost nothing is ugly, not even the things people usually turn away from, such as age or wildness. It's like a nature documentary: hold the camera on a spider's web or an old elephant's skin for long enough, and it becomes beautiful.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Such a man will contemplate in the real world the fierce jaws of wild beasts with no less delight than when sculptors or painters set forth for him their presentments. With like pleasure will his chaste eyes behold the maturity and grace of old age in man or woman, and the inviting charms of youth.

Question: Can a person be happy anywhere?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Wherever one can live, one can live well. One can live in a court, so one can live well there.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes. If it is possible to live somewhere, it is possible to live well there, even in a place full of pressure and politics. It's like a good cook in a small kitchen: the meal depends on the cook far more than on the kitchen.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The soul takes colour from its impressions, therefore steep it in such thoughts as these:—Wherever a man can live, he can live well. A man can live in a court, therefore he can live well there.

Question: How do I feel connected to something bigger?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Think often of the bond of all things and their relation to one another. All are woven together, and one's own part belongs in the web.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Keep reminding yourself that everything is connected, and that your part is woven in with the rest. It's like a single pixel on a screen: tiny alone, and the picture is made of nothing else.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): All things are twined together, in one sacred bond. Scarce is there one thing quite foreign to another. They are all ranged together, and leagued to form the same ordered whole.

Question: How do I cope with losing someone I love?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Loss is nothing but change, and change is the joy of universal nature. What dies does not fall out of the universe.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Loss is a form of change, and change is how the whole of nature works. Nothing that dies drops out of the world. It is taken back into it. It's like autumn leaves: they fall, and by spring the tree is being fed by them. Grief is still allowed. This is a way to hold it, and it takes time.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Loss is naught but change; in change is the joy of universal Nature, and by her all things are ordered well. From the beginning of ages they have been shaped alike, and to all eternity they will be the same.

Question: Will the pain of grief ever ease?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do the mourners still sit at the tombs of those they loved? In time they too were gone. Grief, like everything, passes.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes. Look at history: the mourners who once sat by the graves are themselves long gone, and their grief with them. Everything passes, sorrow included. It's like a deep cut: at first it is all you can feel, and in time it becomes a scar you carry and only sometimes notice.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): And if they were still mourning could their masters be sensible of it? Or if they were sensible of it, would it give them any pleasure? Or if they were pleased with it, could the mourners live for ever?

Question: How do I accept a death that feels unfair?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Death, like birth, is a mystery of nature: elements joined, then loosed again. There is nothing in it to be ashamed of or to resent.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Death belongs to the same natural process as birth: things come together, and later come apart. Nothing in that is shameful or a personal injustice. It's like the tide: it comes in and goes out on a timetable nobody chose, and it is not being unfair to anyone on the beach.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Death, like birth, is a mystery of nature; the one a compounding of elements, the other a resolution into the same. In neither is there anything shameful or against the nature of the rational animal, or contrary to the law of its constitution.

Question: How should I think about losing a child?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He buried children of his own. His counsel is that a child is lent and not owned. Grief of this kind needs people around you as well as principles.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He buried children of his own, so he speaks as a father. His view is that a child is given for a time and never owned, and that every day with them was a gift. It's like a piece of music that ends too early: its shortness takes nothing from how beautiful it was. This is a grief nobody should carry alone, so keep people close.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Epictetus said that, when you kiss your child, you should whisper within yourself: “To-morrow perhaps he may die.” “Ill-omened words”! say you. “The words have no evil omen,”

Question: How do I prepare for losing my parents?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Keep in mind how quickly all are carried off: one buries another and soon follows. Love them now, as people given for a time.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Keep in mind how quickly everyone is carried off, and let that turn into love now. Treat your parents as people you have been given for a limited time. It's like the last week of a holiday: once you know the days are numbered, you stop wasting them and start noticing them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Lucilla buried Verus, and soon followed him to the grave. Secunda saw the death of Maximus, and soon herself died. Epitynchanus buried Diotimus, and then Epitynchanus was buried.

Question: How do I go on living after a loss?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Consider yourself as having died, and treat what remains as a bonus. Live it according to nature.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Imagine your life ended at the moment of the loss, and treat everything after it as extra time you weren't promised. Then live it well. It's like stoppage time in football: the match could have ended, and you have been given more minutes. You play them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Live what yet remains according to Nature's laws, as an overplus granted to you beyond your hope.

Question: How do I let go of something I loved?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Say to nature, who gives and takes back: give what you will, take what you will. Say it without pride, in obedience and goodwill.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Hold everything with an open hand. Say to life, which gives and takes back: give what you choose, take what you choose. Say it without bitterness. It's like holding a small bird: grip it tight to keep it and you harm it. An open palm is the only way to hold it at all.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To Nature, which gives and again resumes all things, the well-instructed, modest man will say: “Give what thou wilt; take again what thou wilt.” And this he says, not with ostentation, but out of pure obedience and good will to Nature.

Question: Why do good people die young?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Many grains of incense fall on the same altar, one sooner and one later. It makes no difference.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Length is not the measure. Every life ends, some earlier and some later, and an early ending does not make a life less complete. It's like a short film beside a three-hour epic: the running time tells you nothing about which one mattered more.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Many grains of frankincense are laid on the same altar. One falls soon, another later. It makes no difference.

Question: How do I support a grieving friend?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Help them as far as you can and as they deserve. Do not be swept away by their feeling, and do not treat the loss as the ruin of a life.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Help as much as you are able, and stay steady yourself. Don't get swept into their grief, and don't speak as though their life is now ruined. It's like a lifeguard: you are no use to a struggling swimmer if you panic too. One calm person in the water is the help.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be not incautiously carried away by sentiment, but aid him that needs it according to your power and his desert. If his need be of the things which are indifferent, think not that he is harmed thereby, for so to think is an evil habit.

Question: How do I remember the dead well?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He began his notebook by naming what each person gave him. Remember the dead by what you learned from them.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He began his own notebook by listing, person by person, what each one gave him. Remember the dead by what you learned from them and still use. It's like a family recipe: every time you cook it the way your grandmother did, she is in the kitchen.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I learned of him accuracy and patience in council, for he never quitted an enquiry satisfied with first impressions. I observed his zeal to retain his friends without being fickle or over fond; his contentment in every condition; his cheerfulness; his forethought about very distant events; his unostentatious attention to the smallest details; his restraint of all popular applause and flattery.

Question: How do I come to terms with a loss that was partly my fault?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Regret is a reproach for having neglected something useful. Take the lesson, and do the next thing rightly.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Regret is useful for one thing: it shows you what you neglected. Take that lesson, then do the next thing properly. It's like a pilot reviewing the flight recorder after a rough landing: the point is the next flight, not endless replay.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Repentance is a self-reproving, because we have neglected something useful. Whatever is good must be useful in some sort, and worthy of the care of a good and honourable man.

Question: How do I accept that everything ends?
Marcus Aurelius would say: All things are for a day: the one who remembers and the one who is remembered.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: In the long view everything lasts only a day: the person remembered and the person remembering. Accepting that is what lets you enjoy things while they are here. It's like cherry blossom: it is loved partly because it falls so soon.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): All things are for a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.

Question: How do I grieve without falling apart?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Feel the blow, since that is natural. Do not add to it the judgement that life is ruined. It is the judgement, more than the event, that breaks a person.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Feel the blow. That is natural, and he doesn't ask you to be made of stone. What to avoid is adding the verdict "my life is ruined", because that verdict breaks people more than the loss does. It's like a broken leg: the pain is real and needs care, and it doesn't mean you will never walk again.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let it not commingle with them, but keep itself apart, and confine these passions to their proper bodily parts; and if they rise into the soul by any sympathy with the body to which it is united, then we must not attempt to resist the sensation, seeing that it is of our nature; but let not the soul, for its part, add thereto the conception that the sensation is good or bad.

Question: I lost my home, my job or my savings. How should I see it?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Receive the gifts of fortune without pride, and part with them without reluctance.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What fortune gives, it can take back. Accept good things without swagger and let them go without clinging. It's like a rented flat: you can live in it fully and enjoy it, while knowing it was never permanently yours.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Receive the gifts of fortune without pride; and part with them without reluctance.

Question: How do I handle the end of a relationship?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Loss is change. Adapt to the lot that has fallen to you, and love the people with whom you are now placed.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The end of a relationship is a change, however much it hurts. Adjust to where life has now put you, and give your care to the people who are actually in it. It's like moving house: you miss the old place, and then you learn the new street and meet the neighbours.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Adapt yourself to the things which your destiny has given you: love those with whom it is your lot to live, and love them with sincere affection.

Question: Is it wrong to still feel sad years later?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He does not forbid feeling. He asks that the ruling mind stay its own master and not add its agreement that the pain is an evil.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. He never forbids feeling. He asks only that your mind stays in charge and doesn't sign off on the idea that the pain is a disaster. It's like an old injury that aches when the weather turns: you notice it, you aren't surprised by it, and you carry on with your day.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let the leading and ruling part of your soul stand unmoved by the stirrings of the flesh, whether gentle or rude.

Question: What should I say to myself at a funeral?
Marcus Aurelius would say: In a little while you will be ashes or bones, and a name, or not even that. What remains? To honour the gods, do good to people, bear and forbear.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Tell yourself the truth: soon you too will be dust and a name, perhaps not even a name. So what is left to do? Respect what is greater than you, be good to people, be patient. It's like a reminder on your calendar: uncomfortable to read, and it is what gets the important thing done.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In a little space you will be only ashes and dry bones and a name, perhaps not even that. A name is but so much empty sound and echo, and the things which are so much prized in life are empty, mean, and rotten.

Question: How do I stop asking "why me?"
Marcus Aurelius would say: Whatever happens to you was prepared for you from all eternity, and the chain of causes was weaving this thread from the beginning.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: This reached you through a long chain of causes that began before you were born. It wasn't aimed at you. It is the part of the pattern that arrived where you stand. It's like rain on a wedding day: the weather wasn't about you. It was weather, and your day was under it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whatever happens to you was prearranged for you from all eternity; and the concatenation of causes had from eternity interwoven your existence with this contingency.

Question: Does anything of a person remain?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He leaves the question open. Whether souls survive or are scattered, what dies is changed and taken back into the whole.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He doesn't claim to know, and says so. Whether a soul survives or disperses, what dies is changed and taken back into the whole, never simply deleted. It's like a drop of water falling into the ocean: you can't point to it any more, and none of it is missing.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If our souls survive us, how, you ask, has the air contained them from eternity? How, I answer, does the earth contain so many bodies buried during so long a time?

Question: How do I find gratitude in grief?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Be thankful for what was given. He counted good parents, a good sister, good teachers and good friends among the gifts of his life.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be thankful for what you were given. He counted the people in his life, parents, sister, teachers, friends, as his real fortune. It's like a full photo album after someone has gone: the sadness is that it ended, and the album is the proof of how much there was.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To the Gods I owe it that I had good grandfathers and parents, a good sister, good teachers, good servants, good kinsmen, and friends, good almost all of them. I have to thank them that I never through haste and rashness offended any of them; though my temper was such as might have led me to it had occasion offered.

Question: How do I come to terms with my own death?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not despise death. Receive it as one of the things nature wills, like growing up and growing old, like teeth and beard and grey hair.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Death is one of the things nature does, in the same list as growing up, going grey and getting old. Meet it as part of the process and not as an enemy. It's like the seasons: nobody treats autumn as a scandal. It is the part of the year that comes next.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): For even as it is to be young, to be old, to grow up, to be full grown; even as it is to breed teeth, and beard, and to grow grey, to beget, to go with child, to be delivered; and to undergo all the effects of nature which life's seasons bring; such is it also to be dissolved in death.

Question: Why does life feel so short?
Marcus Aurelius would say: A human life is an instant, its substance in flux, its fame uncertain. What then can guide a person? One thing only: philosophy.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Life is short, everything in it keeps moving, and reputation is unreliable. The one thing that can steer you through is a clear way of thinking about how to live. It's like a short ferry crossing in rough water: you can't lengthen the trip, and a compass decides whether you arrive anywhere.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The duration of man's life is but an instant; his substance is fleeting, his senses dull; the structure of his body corruptible; the soul but a vortex. We cannot reckon with fortune, or lay our account with fame.

Question: How should knowing I will die change how I live?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do every deed, speak every word and think every thought as one who may leave life at any moment.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Do, say and think everything as someone who could be leaving at any moment. It clears away pettiness quickly. It's like the last day in a job: you stop arguing about small things, you thank people, and you finish what matters.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Do every deed, speak every word, think every thought in the knowledge that you may end your days any moment. To depart from men, if there be really Gods, is nothing terrible.

Question: Is a long life better than a short one?
Marcus Aurelius would say: No one loses any life but the one he is living now. The longest and the shortest come to the same, for the present is all anyone has.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. All anyone ever has is the present moment, and that is the same size for everyone. Nobody can lose years they haven't lived. It's like water from a tap: however big the tank, you can only ever drink the glass that is in your hand.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Though you should live three thousand ears or as many myriads, yet remember that no man loses any other life than that which now lives, nor lives any other than that which he is now losing.

Question: I am afraid I will die before I have done anything that matters.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not order your life as though you had ten thousand years. While you live, while you can, be good.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stop planning as if you had ten thousand years. What matters is available today: be a good person now, while you can. It's like waiting for the perfect moment to call an old friend: the call that counts is the one you make this afternoon.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Order not your life as though you had ten thousand years to live. Fate hangs over you. While you live, while yet you may, be good.

Question: How do I stop obsessing about death?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look closely at each thing you do, and ask whether death is a terror because it takes this away.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Go through your day item by item and ask: is death frightening because it would take this away? For most items the answer is no, and the fear shrinks.
