It's like checking a suitcase before a flight: once you look at what is inside, you find little you couldn't travel without.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Look attentively on each particular thing you do, and ask yourself if death be a terror because it deprives you of this.

Question: What happens when we die?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Either a scattering of atoms or a change into another form. He does not claim to know, and he holds that neither is to be feared.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He doesn't know, and says so plainly. Either everything disperses or it changes into another form, and he holds that neither is something to fear. It's like a sealed envelope: you can't read it yet, and you can still reason that neither of the two possible letters inside is bad news.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Concerning death: If the Universe be a concourse of atoms, death is a scattering of these; if it be an ordered unity, death is an extinction or a translation to another state.

Question: How do I face a terminal diagnosis?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You went aboard, you made the voyage, you have come to harbour. Step ashore. Lean on your doctors and your people as well as on this.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You came aboard, you made the journey, and you are coming into port. That is a complete voyage. It's like a flight coming in to land: the landing is part of the trip, and it isn't the trip going wrong. Lean on your doctors and your people as well as on this. Nobody lands a plane alone.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You have gone aboard, made your voyage, come to harbour. Disembark: if into another life, there will God be also; if into nothingness, at least you will have done with bearing pain and pleasure, and with your slavery to this vessel so much meaner than its slave.

Question: Does it matter that I will be forgotten?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The time is at hand when you will have forgotten everything, and everything will have forgotten you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Soon you will have forgotten everything, and everything will have forgotten you. That frees you: what you do is worth doing for its own sake, with no audience required. It's like a sandcastle: the tide takes it by evening, and the child who built it still had a full, good day.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The time is at hand when you shall forget all things, and when all shall forget you.

Question: How do I make peace with dying after a full life?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Many physicians are dead who knitted their brows over their patients. Pass through this short time according to nature, and end content, as an olive falls when it is ripe.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Many have gone before, including the doctors who fretted over the dying. Live this stretch as nature intends and finish content. It's like the end of a long, good dinner: you put down the napkin, thank the host, and get up from the table satisfied.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Constantly consider how many physicians are dead and gone, who frequently knitted their brows over their patients; how many astrologers, who foretold the deaths of others with great ostentation of their art; how many philosophers, who wrote endlessly on death and immortality; how many warriors, who slew their thousands; and how many tyrants, who used their power of life and death with cruel wantonness, as though they had been immortal.

Question: What is the right attitude on my last day?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Depart satisfied. The one who releases you is satisfied too.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Leave satisfied. The same nature that brought you in is the one letting you go, and it is content with the part you played. It's like the end of a shift: you hand over, hang up the uniform and go home, and the one who drew up the rota is satisfied too.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Depart then graciously; for he who dismisses you is gracious.

Question: Why do people fear death more than a wasted life?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Stop dreading the end of life. Fear instead that you may never begin to live according to nature.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The end is not the thing to dread. The real loss would be to reach it without ever having started to live the way you are meant to. It's like holding a gym membership for years and never going: the sad part isn't the day it expires.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If then, now that you are near your exit, setting behind you all other things, you will hold alone in reverence your ruling part, the spirit divine within you; if you will cease to dread the end of life, but rather fear to miss the beginning of life according to Nature, you will be a man, worthy of the ordered Universe that produced you; you will cease to be a stranger in your own country, gaping in wonder at every daily happening, caught up by this trifle or by that.

Question: How do I live each day fully?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is the perfection of character to spend each day as if it were the last, without excitement, without sloth and without pretence.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Treat each day as though it were the last: no frenzy, no laziness, no pretending. It's like a chef plating a dish for a guest they respect: unhurried, careful, and nothing fake on the plate.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is the perfection of morals to spend each day as if it were the last of life, without excitement, without sloth, and without hypocrisy.

Question: I sometimes feel I cannot go on. What would he say?
Marcus Aurelius would say: His word is to stop looking at the whole of life and take only the next small act. This is also the moment to tell a doctor or someone you trust, today. He took help without shame.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stop looking at the whole of life. Take only the next small thing: a glass of water, a shower, one phone call. That is all this hour asks. It's like carrying something far too heavy: you put it down, and you call someone to take the other end. Tell a doctor or someone you trust today. He took help without shame.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Do not confound yourself by considering the whole of life, and by dwelling upon the multitude and greatness of the pains and troubles to which you may probably be exposed.

Question: How do I console myself that even the great die?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Alexander of Macedon and his mule-driver came to the same condition when they died.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Death is the great leveller: the conqueror and the man who drove his mules ended in the same condition. It's like the end of a chess game: the king and the pawn go back into the same box.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Alexander of Macedon and his muleteer, when they died, were in a like condition. They were either alike resumed into the seminal source of all things, or alike dispersed among the atoms.

Question: How do I prepare for death in practice?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Consider how death should find you, in body and in soul. Think of the shortness of life and of the gulf of time behind and before.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Think now about how you want to be found: what state your affairs are in, and what state your character is in. And remember how brief life is against the time before and after it. It's like packing the night before a trip: you sleep better, and the morning isn't a scramble.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Consider how death ought to find you, both as to body and as to soul. Think of the shortness of life, of the eternities before and after, and of the infirmity of all material things.

Question: Is death an evil?
Marcus Aurelius would say: What does not make a person worse does not make his life worse. Death and life, honour and dishonour, come to good and bad alike, so they are neither good nor evil.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. Whatever doesn't make you a worse person doesn't make your life worse. Death comes to good and bad people alike, so it can't be a punishment or a reward. It's like the final whistle: it blows for the winning and the losing team alike, so it can't be a verdict on either.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): She could not fail us so completely that, either from want of power or want of skill, good and evil should happen promiscuously to good men and to bad alike. Now death and life, glory and reproach, pain and pleasure, riches and poverty—all these happen equally to the good and to the bad.

Question: How do I use the thought of death to live better?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You may end your days at any moment. Let that decide what you do and say and think today.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You could go at any time. Let that fact choose what you do, say and think today. It's like a phone on low battery: you stop opening pointless apps and save what is left for the call that matters.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Do every deed, speak every word, think every thought in the knowledge that you may end your days any moment. To depart from men, if there be really Gods, is nothing terrible.

Question: What if there is nothing after death?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Then there is nothing to feel and nothing to fear. The soul that stands ready to be extinguished, scattered or to continue is the happy one.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Then there is nothing to feel, and so nothing to fear. The happiest mind is one that is ready for any of the outcomes. It's like the years before you were born: you weren't there for them, and they caused you no trouble at all.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How happy is the soul that stands ready to part from the body when it must, and either to be extinguished or to be scattered, or to survive! But let this readiness arise from individual judgment, not from mere obstinacy, as with the Christians, but deliberately, with dignity, and with no affected air of tragedy; so that others may be led to a like disposition.

Question: How should I leave things with the people around me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: No one is so fortunate that someone will not be glad when he dies. Leave them anyway as you lived: kindly, gently, without being torn away.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't expect everyone to mourn. Some will be relieved, whoever you are. Leave them anyway the way you lived with them: kindly, gently, without a struggle. It's like leaving a party: you don't need every guest to beg you to stay. You thank the host and go warmly.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): On the other hand, depart from your fellow-men, not as if torn away; but let your going be like that of one who dies an easy death, whose soul is gently released from the body.

Question: How do I cope with chronic pain?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Pain that cannot be borne carries us off. Pain that lasts can be borne. The mind keeps its calm by withdrawing, and the ruling part is not made worse.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Pain that is truly unbearable ends itself, and pain that lasts is pain you are bearing. The mind can step back from it and stay itself. It's like a loud neighbour: the noise comes through the wall, and it still doesn't own the house. You decide what happens in your rooms.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Concerning pain: Pain which cannot be borne brings us deliverance. Pain that lasts musts needs be bearable. The mind can abstract itself from the body, and the soul takes no hurt.

Question: How do I stay steady when I am ill?
Marcus Aurelius would say: In his sickness Epicurus did not talk about his body. He went on with philosophy. Do the same, and do not let the mind chatter with the body about its troubles.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: When you are ill, keep doing the things that make you who you are, and don't let illness become your only topic. It's like a radio stuck on one station: your body's complaints will play all day if you let them. You can change the channel to something worth hearing.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Epicurus says: “In my sickness my conversations were not about the diseases of this poor body; nor did I speak of any such things to those who came to me. I continued to discourse as before on the principles of natural Philosophy, and was chiefly intent on the problem of how the mind, though it partakes in the violent commotions of the flesh, might remain undisturbed and keep guard on its own proper excellence.

Question: I hate how my body looks.
Marcus Aurelius would say: "You are a poor soul carrying a corpse," said Epictetus. The body is the vessel. The worth of a person lies in what steers it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The body is the vehicle. What gives a person worth is whatever is doing the steering. It's like judging a driver by the paintwork on the car: the scratches say nothing about how well it is driven.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): “Thou art a poor soul, saddled with a corpse,” said Epictetus.

Question: How do I accept getting older?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The mind may fail before life does. So hurry: death comes nearer each day, and the power to understand may leave first.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ageing isn't only about the body. The clear thinking you rely on may fade before life does, so use it now. It's like a voucher with an expiry date you can't read: the sensible thing is to spend it today.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let him be up and doing then, not only because death comes nearer every day, but because understanding and intelligence often leave us before we die.

Question: How do I deal with a new diagnosis?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Say only what the first report says: this has been found. Do not add "and it is a disaster". Then follow what your doctors prescribe.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Say only what the report says: this has been found. Don't add "and my life is over". Then do what your doctors prescribe. It's like a warning light on a dashboard: it tells you to visit the garage. It does not tell you the car is finished.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Dwell thus upon first appearances; add nothing to them from within, and no harm befalls you: or rather add the recognition that all is part of the world's lot.

Question: How should I think about a treatment I have been prescribed?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Take what the doctor orders in the same spirit as what life orders. Each is prescribed toward a larger health, even when it is bitter.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Take a treatment in the same spirit as you take what life hands you: prescribed toward a larger health, even when it tastes bitter. It's like physiotherapy after an injury: the exercises hurt, and they are how the knee comes back.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Conceive therefore that, for Nature, the doing of her work and the fulfilling of her purposes are, as it were, her health; and welcome all that happens, even should it seem hard fortune, because it tends to the health of the Universe, and to the prosperity and felicity of Zeus.

Question: How do I stop pain taking over my mind?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let the ruling part stay unmoved by the stirrings of the flesh. Keep those feelings in their own region and do not add the opinion that they are evil.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Let the pain stay where it is, in the body, and don't add the opinion that it is a catastrophe. The thinking part can remain unmoved. It's like background noise in a café: you can't switch it off, and you can still decline to hand it the microphone.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let the leading and ruling part of your soul stand unmoved by the stirrings of the flesh, whether gentle or rude.

Question: How do I cope with disability or a lost ability?
Marcus Aurelius would say: No one can hinder the proper work of the mind. Fire, sword, tyrant and slander cannot reach it. What the body has lost, the mind has not.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Nothing can stop the mind from doing its proper work. What the body has lost, the mind has not. It's like a pianist who loses the use of a hand and turns to composing: the music was never in the hand.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): No man can hinder the proper work of the mind. Nor fire, nor sword, nor tyrant, nor calumny can reach it, nor any other thing, when it is become even as a sphere, complete and perfect within itself.

Question: How do I handle being tired all the time?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is a shame for the soul to give in while the body still holds out. Yet take regular, moderate care of the body, as Antoninus did. If it persists, see a doctor.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't let the spirit quit while the body can still go on. But look after the body sensibly too, as his adoptive father did. It's like a phone battery: you push on through the day, and you still plug it in at night. If the tiredness doesn't lift, see a doctor.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is shame and dishonour that, in any man's life, the soul should faint from its duty while the body still holds out.

Question: How much should I care about fitness and appearance?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Take regular but moderate care of the body: not as one too fond of life or of looks, and not as one who despises them.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look after your body steadily and in moderation. Not as someone obsessed with looks or long life, and not as someone who neglects it. It's like servicing a car: regular oil changes, yes. Polishing it every evening, no.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He took regular but moderate care of his body, neither as one over fond of life or of the adornment of his person, nor as one who despised these things. Thus, through his own care, he seldom needed any medicines, whether salves or potions.

Question: How do I cope with a long illness?
Marcus Aurelius would say: In all pain remember that there is nothing shameful in it and that it cannot harm the mind that guides you. Most pains are bearable when imagination adds nothing.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Remember that there is nothing shameful in being ill and that it cannot damage your character. Much of the suffering comes from what imagination adds. It's like a long-haul flight: uncomfortable and slow, and bearable hour by hour once you stop counting how many are left.

Question: How do I face surgery or a frightening procedure?

Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You will come to it, if need be, with the same power to reason, as you use upon your present business.

Question: How do I care for a sick relative without resentment?
Marcus Aurelius would say: No one wearies of what brings him gain, and acting according to nature is gain. Do not tire, then, of gaining by giving.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Giving care is itself a gain to the giver, because it is exactly what a human being is for. So don't tire of receiving by giving. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): No man wearies of what brings him gain, and your gain lies in acting according to nature. Be not weary, therefore, of gaining by the act which gives others gain.

Question: What is a healthy attitude to food?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look at it plainly: this is the dead body of a fish, this of a bird or a pig. The plain description cuts through to what the thing is.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at food for what it plainly is, without the menu language. Seeing it bare breaks the spell it has over you. It's like reading the ingredients label on the back of the packet and ignoring the picture on the front.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Keep these thoughts for meats and eatables: This that is before me is the dead carcase of a fish, a fowl, a hog. This Falernian is but a little grape juice. Think of your purple robes as sheep's wool stained in the blood of a shell-fish.

Question: Is it all right to enjoy good food and wine?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Yes, with mastery. Like Socrates, be able both to abstain and to enjoy the things most people are too weak to go without and too greedy to use with restraint.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes, as long as you are the one in charge. Be able to enjoy it and equally able to go without. It's like dessert in a restaurant: a pleasure when you choose it, and a problem only when you can't say no.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): A man might fairly apply that to him which is recorded of Socrates: that he could both abstain from and enjoy these things, in want whereof many show themselves weak, and, in the possession, intemperate.

Question: How do I handle a mental health struggle?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He would say the mind has a refuge within itself. He also took help without shame, as a soldier is helped up a wall. Use both: principles and a professional.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The mind has a place of calm within itself, and he also took help without any shame, the way a soldier is helped up a wall. Use both. It's like a broken arm: you rest it yourself, and you also let a doctor set it. Nobody calls the plaster cast a weakness.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Reflect that the mind, once withdrawn within itself, once grown conscious of its own power, has no concern with the motions, rough or smooth, of the breathing body. Remember, too, all that you have heard and assented to concerning pain and pleasure.

Question: How do I stop assuming every symptom is serious?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Tell yourself only what the appearance directly reports, and add nothing from within.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Report to yourself only what the symptom actually shows, and add nothing. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Dwell thus upon first appearances; add nothing to them from within, and no harm befalls you: or rather add the recognition that all is part of the world's lot.

Question: How do I accept physical decline gracefully?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Even what comes with age has its own bloom to the eye that can see it: the ripeness of an old man or woman.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Age has its own kind of beauty for anyone who knows how to look. It's like an old leather bag or a well-used wooden table: the marks are what make it better than the new one.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): With like pleasure will his chaste eyes behold the maturity and grace of old age in man or woman, and the inviting charms of youth. Question: How do I keep my dignity when my body fails?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Bear toil and pain without acting the wretch, and without courting pity or admiration.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Bear it without self-pity and without performing for sympathy or praise. It's like an older athlete who can no longer sprint and still walks onto the pitch with their head up: the dignity was never in the speed.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Bear toil and pain, not as if wretched under it, nor as courting pity or admiration. Wish for one thing only; always to act or to refrain as social wisdom requires.

Question: Should I fear losing my mind as I age?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He names that fear exactly: the power to understand may go before the body does. His answer is to use the mind well now.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He names that fear himself: understanding may go before the body does. His answer is to use your mind well today, on what matters. It's like daylight on a winter afternoon: you can't keep it, so you do the reading while there is light.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): But self-command, accurate appreciation of duty, power to scrutinize what strikes his senses, or even to decide whether he should take his departure, all powers, indeed, which demand a well-trained understanding, must be extinguished in him.

Question: Why do I care more about other people's opinions than my own?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Each of us loves himself above all others, yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on theirs. He found this astonishing.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: It is a strange fact: everyone loves themselves most, and still trusts other people's opinion of them more than their own. Notice it, and it loosens. It's like owning the house and asking passers-by whether you are allowed to like the kitchen.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I have wondered often how it comes that, while every man loves himself beyond all others, yet he holds his own opinion of himself in less esteem than the opinion of others.

Question: How do I build self-respect?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Never value anything that would make you break your word, lose your honour, hate, suspect, curse, or pretend.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Decide what you will never trade: your word, your honour, your honesty. Self-respect is built from the deals you refuse. It's like a shop with a "not for sale" sign on one item: that item tells you what the owner values most.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Never esteem aught of advantage which will oblige you to break your faith, or to desert your honour; to hate, to suspect, or to execrate any man; to play a part; or to set your mind on anything that needs to be hidden by wall or curtain.

Question: I feel like I am not good enough.
Marcus Aurelius would say: You may not be admired for sharpness of wit. Show then what is wholly in your power: sincerity, dignity, endurance, contentment, kindness, freedom from pettiness.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You may never be the cleverest person in the room. So lead with what is entirely up to you: sincerity, dignity, stamina, contentment, kindness. It's like a footballer without great pace: effort, positioning and attitude are free, and managers build teams around them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Display these; they are wholly in your power. Be sincere, be dignified, be painstaking; scorn pleasure, repine not at fate, need little; be kind and frank; love not exaggeration and vain talk; strive after greatness.

Question: How do I stop needing validation?
Marcus Aurelius would say: What is beautiful is beautiful in itself, and praise is no part of it. Is an emerald worse for not being praised?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A good thing is good in itself. Praise adds nothing to it and silence takes nothing away. It's like a photo you posted that got no likes: it is the same photo, exactly as good as it was before you checked.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Nothing is the better or the worse for being praised; and this holds also of what is beautiful in the common estimation: of material forms and works of art. Thus true beauty needs nothing beyond itself, any more than law, or truth, or kindness, or honour.

Question: How do I deal with impostor syndrome?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not be ashamed of taking help. Your task is to do your part, like a soldier storming a wall: if lame, you climb with another's hand.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Needing help doesn't make you a fraud. Your job is to do your part, and if you can't do it alone you do it with someone's hand. It's like a new driver using a satnav: you are still the one driving, and you still arrive.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is laid upon you to do your part, as on a soldier when the wall is stormed. What, then, if you are lame, and cannot scale the battlements alone, but can with another's help?

Question: How do I stop being so hard on myself?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not fret or despond when you fall short. Come back to your principles as one with sore eyes returns to the sponge, and not as a pupil to a master.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: When you fall short, don't punish yourself. Go back to your principles for relief, the way you go back to a remedy, and not the way a pupil goes back to an angry teacher. It's like a spell-checker: it underlines the word in red, you fix it, and it never calls you stupid.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Love the good to which you return; and come back to Philosophy, not as one who comes to a master, but as one whose eyes ache recurs to sponge and egg, as another has recourse to plasters, or a third to fomentation.

Question: How do I become confident?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is in your power to live above all compulsion, in the greatest calm of mind, though the whole world cry out against you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Confidence comes from knowing that your calm and your choices are yours, even if everyone around you objects. It's like a goalkeeper in front of a hostile crowd: thousands are shouting, and none of them is allowed on the pitch.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is in your power to live superior to all violence, and in the greatest calm of mind, were all men to rail against you as they pleased; and though wild beasts were to tear asunder the wretched members of this fleshly mass which has grown with your growth.

Question: How do I know my own worth?
Marcus Aurelius would say: A person's worth is just the worth of what he pursues. Ask what you are pursuing.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You are worth what you spend your life chasing. So look at what you are chasing. It's like a bank statement: it shows what you value more truthfully than anything you say about yourself.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is then your duty amid all this to stand firm, kindly and not proud, yet to understand that a man's worth is just the worth of that which he pursues.

Question: What makes a person valuable?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Not breathing, feeling, or being applauded. What is worth valuing is to act and to hold back according to one's own constitution.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Not being alive, not feeling things, not being applauded. What counts is acting, and holding back, in line with what you are built to be. It's like a knife: its value is that it cuts well, not that it sits in a display case collecting compliments.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To feel the impressions of sense, to be swayed like puppets by passion, to herd together and to live by bread; all this is no great thing. There is nothing here superior to our power of discharging our superfluous food.

Question: How do I stop being a people-pleaser?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let anyone say or do what he pleases, I must be good: just as an emerald keeps its colour whatever anyone says or does.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Whatever anyone says or does, your job is to stay good, the way a gemstone keeps its colour. It's like a thermostat compared with a thermometer: one just reflects the room, and the other holds its setting whatever the room is doing.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let any one say or do what he pleases, I must be a good man. It is just as gold, or emeralds, or purple might say continually: “Let men do or say what they please, I must be an emerald, and retain my lustre”.

Question: How do I trust my own judgement?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Hold in honour the faculty that forms opinions. On it alone depends whether any opinion arises that is contrary to nature and reason.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Respect the part of you that forms judgements, and look after it. Everything else depends on whether it is working well. It's like the compass on a ship: you check it, you keep it away from magnets, and then you trust it over the opinions of the passengers.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Hold in honour the faculty which forms opinions. It depends on this faculty alone that no opinion your soul entertains be inconsistent with the nature and constitution of the rational being.

Question: I feel ashamed of who I have been. Can I change?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Within ten days you will seem a god to those who now think you a beast, if you return to your principles and to reason.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes, and faster than you think. Go back to your principles and act on them, and within days the people who wrote you off will see someone else. It's like a restaurant under new management: a few good meals, and the old reviews stop mattering.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Within ten days, if you return to the observance of moral principles and to the cult of reason, you will appear a God to them who now esteem you a wild beast or an ape.

Question: How do I stop pretending to be someone I am not?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Be upright, either by nature or by correction.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be straight, either because it comes naturally or because you corrected yourself into it. Either way counts. It's like a filter on a photo: sooner or later people meet you in person, so you may as well post the real one.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be upright either by nature or by correction.

Question: How do I accept my flaws?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is ridiculous not to flee the fault in oneself, which is possible, and to try to flee the faults of others, which is not. Start with what is yours to mend.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Start with your own faults, because those can be fixed. Trying to escape everyone else's is impossible. It's like tidying your own room and leaving off complaining about the state of the street.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is ridiculous that you flee not from the vice that is in yourself, as you have it in your power to do; but are still striving to flee from the vice in others, which you can never do.

Question: What if I have no special talent?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Love the art you have learned, humble though it be, and find your rest in it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Love the skill you have, however modest, and settle into it. It's like a local plumber everyone recommends: no awards, no television show, and a full diary because the work is good.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Love the art which you have learned, humble though it be, and in it find your recreation. And spend the remainder of your life as one who with all his heart commits his concerns to the Gods, and neither acts the tyrant nor the slave to any of mankind.

Question: How do I stop feeling inferior around successful people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Alexander, Caesar, Pompey: what were they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus, Socrates? The latter knew things and their causes. The former were slaves to many cares.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Measure success properly. The conquerors were ruled by endless worries. The thinkers understood things and were their own masters. It's like comparing the busiest person in the office with the calmest: a full calendar is no proof of the better life.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Alexander, Caesar, Pompey, what were they compared with Diogenes, Heraclitus, Socrates? These knew the nature of things, their causes and their matter, and the minds within them were at one.

Question: How do I become my own person?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let the god within you be the guardian of a grown, living being who has taken his post. Stand upright, and do not need to be propped upright.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stand up straight under your own power, and don't rely on other people's approval to hold you up. It's like a tent and a tree: one stays up only while the ropes hold, and the other stands because of its own roots.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let the God within direct you as a manly being, as an elder, a statesman, a Roman, and a ruler, standing prepared like one who awaits the recall from life, in marching order; requiring neither an oath nor the testimony of any man.

Question: How do I stop seeking approval from people who do not matter?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do you wish to be praised by a man who curses himself three times an hour?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at who you are trying to impress. Would you want praise from someone who is unhappy with himself three times an hour? It's like asking for restaurant tips from a person who hates every meal they eat.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Do you wish to be praised by a man who curses himself thrice within an hour? Can you desire to please one who is not pleased with himself? Can he be pleased with himself who repents of almost everything he does?

Question: Is it selfish to focus on myself?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Seldom is anyone unhappy for not watching what is in another's mind. Those who do not watch the movements of their own must be unhappy.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. People are rarely unhappy because they failed to watch what others think. They are unhappy when they fail to watch their own mind. It's like the safety briefing on a plane: fit your own oxygen mask first, and then you are of use to anyone else.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Seldom are any found unhappy from not observing what is in the minds of others. But such as observe not well the stirrings of their own souls must of necessity be unhappy.

Question: How do I respect myself after being humiliated?
Marcus Aurelius would say: None of them can involve you in anything shameful. What does not make a person worse does not harm him.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Humiliation can't make you a worse person, and only what makes you worse can really harm you. Nobody else's behaviour can put shame into you. It's like someone spilling a drink on your jacket: the stain is on the jacket. You are not the jacket.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I therefore cannot be hurt by any of these, since none of them can involve me in any baseness. I cannot be angry with my brother, or sever myself from him, for we are made by nature for mutual assistance, like the feet, the hands, the eyelids, the upper and lower rows of teeth.

Question: How do I handle criticism?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If anyone can show that I think or act wrongly, I will gladly change. I seek the truth, by which no one was ever harmed.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If someone can show you that you are wrong, change gladly. You are after the truth, and the truth has never hurt anyone. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If any one can convince or shew me that I am wrong in thought or deed, I will gladly change. It is truth that I seek; and truth never yet hurt any man. What does hurt is persistence in error or in ignorance.

Question: How do I deal with unfair criticism?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Go into their minds and see what kind of people they are. There is no need to be anxious about what they think of you. Yet stay kind to them.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at who the critics are and how they think. You don't need to worry about their opinion, and you can still treat them kindly. It's like a one-star review from someone who was angry about the weather: read it, see where it comes from, and wish them well.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You will see that you need not trouble yourself to make him think well or ill of you. Yet you should be kindly towards such men, for they are by nature your friends: and the Gods, too, aid them in all ways; by dreams, by oracles, and even in the things about which they are most eager.

Question: What if people gossip about me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let them look to that. Look to it yourself that nothing you do or say deserves it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What they say is their business. Yours is to make sure nothing you do deserves it. It's like a rumour that a shop cheats its customers: the reply that works is every customer walking out with the right change.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): And let me look to it that I be found doing or saying nothing worthy of his contempt. Does any one hate me? That is his affair. I shall be kind and good-natured to every one, and ready to shew his mistake to him that hates me; not in order to upbraid him, or to make a show of my patience, but from genuine goodness, like Phocion, if he indeed was sincere.

Question: How do I stop caring about my reputation?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look at the minds of those who praise, and how quickly all is forgotten. The whole earth is a point, and the place you live a corner of it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at who is doing the praising and how fast it is all forgotten. The world is tiny in the scheme of things, and your corner of it tinier. It's like last year's trending topics: try to name three. That is how long the crowd's attention lasts.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): All the earth is but a point in the Universe; how small a corner of that little is inhabited, and even there how few are they and of how little worth who are to praise us!

Question: Someone lied about me. What should I do?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is a king's part to do good and be spoken ill of.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Doing right and being spoken badly of often go together, especially for anyone with responsibility. It's like a parent who says no to sweets before dinner: unpopular for an hour, and right.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is a saying of Antisthenes, that it is the part of a king to do good and reap reproach.

Question: How do I respond to hate online?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not judge as the one who insults you judges, or as he wishes you to judge. See the thing as it truly is.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't adopt the view of the person insulting you, and don't see things the way they want you to. Look at what is actually true. It's like a comment section: a stranger's typing doesn't become a fact because it appears under your name.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Think not as your insulter judges or wishes you to judge: but see things as they truly are.

Question: Should I defend myself or stay quiet?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not be turned aside by the blame or talk that may follow. If the thing is good to do or say, do not judge it unworthy of you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't let the fear of talk decide for you. If a thing is right to say or do, it is worthy of you, so say or do it. It's like pointing out, in a meeting, the mistake everyone has noticed: the awkward moment passes, and the mistake gets fixed.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Judge no speech or action unworthy of you which is consistent with nature. Be not dissuaded by any consequent criticism or censure from others; but, if the speech or action be honourable, judge yourself worthy to say or do it.

Question: How do I take feedback without getting defensive?
Marcus Aurelius would say: To change your course and follow one who sets you right is still your own free act. It comes from your own judgement.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Changing your mind because someone showed you a better way is still your own decision, made by your own judgement. It's like accepting a suggested edit in a document: the document is still yours, and now it is better.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember that to change your course, and to follow any man who can set you right is no compromise of your freedom. The act is your own, performed on your own impulse and judgment, and according to your own understanding.

Question: How do I know whose opinion to listen to?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Listen to anyone who can show you wrong by reason. As for the rest, consider what kind of people they are whose approval you want.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Listen to anyone who can show you, with reasons, where you are wrong. For the rest, look at what sort of people they are before you chase their approval. It's like medical advice: you listen to the one who examined you, not to the loudest voice in the waiting room.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Consider constantly what manner of men they are whose approbation you desire, and what may be the character of their souls. Then you will neither accuse such as err unwillingly, nor need their commendation when you look into the springs of their opinions and their desires.

Question: What if people think I am strange for living differently?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let people see a person living according to nature. If they cannot bear him, so be it. Better that than to live as they do.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Let people see someone living by what is right. If they can't stand it, so be it. That is better than living as they do in order to blend in. It's like being the first person on your street to cycle to work: a few raised eyebrows, and you carry on pedalling.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let men see and know you as a man indeed, living according to Nature. If they cannot endure you, let them slay you. It is better so than to live as they live.

Question: How do I handle being misunderstood?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is quite possible to be a godlike person and to be recognised by no one.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You can be an excellent person and go completely unrecognised. Goodness doesn't need an audience to be real. It's like the engineer who designed the bridge you cross every day: you will never know the name, and the bridge holds.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is very possible to be a God among men, and yet be recognised by none. Remember that always, and this as well, that the happiness of life lies in very few things. And though you despair of becoming great in Logic or in Science, you need not despair of becoming a free man, full of modesty and unselfishness, and of obedience unto God.

Question: Does a good reputation matter?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Those who chase fame after death forget that those who remember them will also die, and so on, until memory is put out.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Not as much as people think. Those who remember you will die too, and those after them, until the memory is gone. It's like a name carved on a park bench: it lasts a while, it weathers, and one day the bench is replaced.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He who is careful and troubled about the fame which is to live after him considers not that each one of those who remember him must very soon die himself, and thereafter also the succeeding generation, until every memory of him, handed on by excited and ephemeral admirers, dies utterly away.

Question: How should I handle praise?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Praise makes nothing better or worse. Is gold, ivory or a flower the better for being praised?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Praise changes nothing about the thing praised. A good thing was already good. It's like a five-star rating on a film: the film was finished before the stars arrived, and they didn't add a single scene.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Nothing is the better or the worse for being praised; and this holds also of what is beautiful in the common estimation: of material forms and works of art. Thus true beauty needs nothing beyond itself, any more than law, or truth, or kindness, or honour.

Question: How do I cope with being publicly shamed?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Take me up and cast me where you will. There I shall keep the spirit within me serene, content if it acts in keeping with its nature.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Wherever you are thrown, you can keep your inner calm, as long as you keep acting in line with your character. It's like a cork pushed under water: wherever it is pushed, it comes back up, because that is what it is made of.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Take me up and cast me where you will; I shall have my own divinity within me serene, that is, satisfied while its every state and action is according to the law of its proper constitution.

Question: How do I give criticism kindly?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Show the mistake gently, without sarcasm or reproach, with affection and no bitterness, as one speaking in private and not for an audience.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Point out the mistake gently: no sarcasm, no blame, with warmth, in private, and never to impress onlookers. It's like a driving instructor with a nervous learner: a calm voice, one correction at a time, and no audience in the back seat.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): But this must be done without irony or reproach, rather with loving-kindness and no bitterness of spirit; not as though you were reading him a lesson, or seeking admiration from any bystander, but as if you designed your remarks for him alone, though others may be present.

Question: How do I correct someone without humiliating them?
Marcus Aurelius would say: As Alexander the grammarian did: never pounce on the mistake. Bring in the right expression tactfully, in an answer or a shared inquiry.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't jump on the error. Use the right version yourself, naturally, in your reply, and let them hear it. It's like a toddler who says "I goed to the park": you answer "you went to the park? Lovely", and they learn without being shamed.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Rather was I dexterously to pronounce the words rightly in my answer, confining approval or objection to the matter itself, and avoiding discussion of the expression, or to use some other form of courteous suggestion.

Question: What if the criticism is true?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Then the fault is mine to remove. The harm lies in staying in error and ignorance, and not in being corrected.

Question: How do I stop replaying an insult?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Things stand outside us and declare nothing about themselves. We write the judgement. Do not write it, and there is no injury.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Events don't come with labels. You write the label, and the insult only lives as long as you keep rewriting it. It's like a voicemail: it was left once, and every other time you heard it, you were the one who pressed play.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Things stand without, by themselves, neither knowing or declaring aught to us concerning themselves. What is it then that pronounces upon them? The ruling part.

Question: How do I handle a bad performance review?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask first whether it is true. If so, mend it. If not, the mistake is theirs. Either way no harm reaches the mind.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask first whether it is true. If it is, fix it. If it isn't, the mistake is theirs. In neither case has your mind been harmed. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If any one can convince or shew me that I am wrong in thought or deed, I will gladly change. It is truth that I seek; and truth never yet hurt any man. What does hurt is persistence in error or in ignorance.

Question: What should I do when I am praised more than I deserve?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Take care not to be turned into a Caesar and dyed with that colour. Keep your simplicity, your goodness and your sincerity.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be careful not to start believing your own publicity. Stay simple, good and sincere. It's like a waiter praised by a table in very high spirits: say thank you, and keep carrying the plates the way you always did.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Guard your simplicity, your goodness, your sincerity, your dignity, your reticence, your love of justice, your piety, your kindliness, your affection for your kin, and your constancy to your duty.

Question: How do I deal with difficult people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: In the morning tell yourself: today I shall meet the meddler, the ungrateful, the insolent. We were made to work together, like the upper and lower rows of teeth.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Expect them. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Say this to yourself in the morning: Today I shall have to do with meddlers, with the ungrateful, with the insolent, with the crafty, with the envious and the selfish. All these vices have beset them, because they know not what is good and what is evil.

Question: How do I deal with ungrateful people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: When you have done good, what more do you want? You acted according to your nature. Does the eye demand a reward for seeing?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If you did something good, you already have what you came for. You acted according to your nature. It's like holding a door open: you do it because that is how you behave, not to collect a thank-you from each person who walks through.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Is it not enough for you that you have acted in this according to your nature? Do you ask a reward for it? It is as if the eye were to ask a reward for seeing, or the feet for walking.

Question: How do I deal with a liar or a cheat?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Can the world exist without shameless people? It cannot. Then do not ask for the impossible. This is one of those who must exist.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A world without dishonest people doesn't exist, so don't demand one. This person is one of those who were always going to turn up. It's like spam email: you don't take it personally. You expect it, filter it, and guard your details.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): When you are offended by the shamelessness of any man, straightway ask yourself: Can the world exist without shameless men? It cannot. Therefore do not demand what is impossible.

Question: How do I deal with arrogant people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Picture them eating, sleeping and the rest. Then picture them lording it, or angry and scolding from their height.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Picture them doing the ordinary things everyone does: eating, sleeping, getting ready in the morning. Then picture them giving orders from on high. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): What sort of men are they when they are eating, sleeping, procreating, easing nature, and the like? Then see them lording it over their fellows, puffed up with pride, angry, or issuing judgments from on high!

Question: How do I handle a toxic family member?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Nature gave a virtue against each fault: against the unkind, gentleness. If it truly cannot be mended, another's wrong must be left with him.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: For every fault in others there is a matching strength in you. Against unkindness, it is gentleness. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is useful also to have this reflection ready: What virtue has nature given to man wherewith to combat this fault? Against unreason she has given meekness as an antidote; against another weakness another power.

Question: How do I deal with someone who refuses to change?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If you can, teach them better. If you cannot, remember that charity was given you for this.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Teach them if you can. If you can't, this is the very situation that kindness and patience exist for. It's like a gardener with a slow plant: you water it and give it light, and you don't shout at it for not growing.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If not, remember that the virtue of charity was given you to be used in such a case. Nay, the Gods are patient with them, and even aid them in their pursuit of some things such as health, wealth, and glory, so gracious are they!

Question: When should I step away from someone?
Marcus Aurelius would say: In the gymnasium we keep clear of a rough opponent without hating him. In life too one may keep out of someone's way, without suspicion or ill will.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You can keep your distance without hating anyone. In a gym people avoid a rough sparring partner and bear no grudge. It's like changing lanes when the car behind is tailgating: no rage, no gesture. You give them room and drive on.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As I said, we may keep out of their way, but without suspicion or hatred.

Question: How do I stop being manipulated?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not be dragged about like a puppet by every selfish pull. The thing that moves the strings is hidden within you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't let yourself be pulled around by every tug on your feelings. The strings are inside you, which means you can see them. It's like a sales call that creates sudden urgency: once you recognise the technique, it stops working.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As to this, take heed, now that you are old, that it remain no longer in servitude; that it be no more dragged hither and thither like a puppet by every selfish impulse. Repine no more at what fate now sends, nor dread what may befall you hereafter.

Question: How do I handle people who drain me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not spend what remains of life in thoughts about others, unless it serves some common good.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't spend your remaining life thinking about what others are doing, unless it serves some shared good. It's like an app running in the background: you never open it, and it is still draining the battery. Close it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Waste not what remains of life in consideration about others, when it makes not for the common good. Be sure you are neglecting other work if you busy yourself with what such a one is doing and why, with what he is saying, thinking, or scheming.

Question: How do I argue well?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Try to persuade them. But act even against their will when justice requires it. If force blocks you, keep calm and use the obstacle for another virtue.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Try to persuade. If justice requires it, act even when they disagree. And if you are blocked by force, stay calm and use the obstacle to practise something else, such as patience. It's like a chess player: you make your best move, and when it is blocked you look for the next one without tipping over the board.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Should one oppose you by force, act with resignation, and shew not that you are hurt, use the obstruction for the exercise of some other virtue, and remember that your purpose involved the reservation that you were not to aim at impossibilities.

Question: How do I work with someone I dislike?
Marcus Aurelius would say: We are all working on one task together, some knowingly, some without knowing it. Even the sleeper is a fellow worker.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You are both working on the same job, whether or not you both know it. Everyone contributes, even the person who seems to be doing nothing. It's like two people rowing the same boat: you don't have to be friends for the boat to reach the shore, and you do both have to row.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): We are all co-operating in one great work, some with knowledge and understanding, others ignorantly and without design. It is in this sense, I think, that Heraclitus says that men are working even while they sleep, working together in all that is being done in the Universe.

Question: How do I deal with betrayal?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Does another wrong me? Let him look to that. His character and his actions are his own. I have what nature wills me to have and I do what my nature wills.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If someone wrongs you, that is on them. Their character and choices are theirs. You still have everything nature gave you, and your own conduct to attend to. It's like a driver who runs a red light and dents your car: the penalty goes on their licence, not yours.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Does another wrong me? Let him look to that. His character and his actions are his own. So much is in my present possession as is dispensed to me by the nature of things, and I act as my own nature now bids me.

Question: How do I deal with people who talk behind my back?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Although they despise one another, they flatter one another. Wishing to rise above one another, they bow to one another.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: See the game for what it is: people who look down on each other flatter each other, and people competing with each other bow to each other. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Although they despise, yet they flatter one another. Although they desire to overtop, yet they cringe to one another.

Question: How do I stop judging people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: When you think someone has done wrong, ask: how do I know this is a wrong? And if it is, how do I know he has not already condemned himself?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Before judging, ask two things: how do I know this is actually wrong? And if it is, how do I know they haven't already judged themselves harder than I could? It's like walking into a film halfway through: you have seen one scene, and you don't yet know the story.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): When you have the impression that a man has sinned, say to yourself: “How do I know that this is sin?” And, if he has sinned, consider that he stands self-condemned: and thus, as it were, has torn his own face.

Question: How do I deal with someone who never listens?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Practise listening closely yourself, and enter as far as you can into the mind of the speaker.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Start by doing the thing yourself. Listen closely, and try to get inside the speaker's thinking. People who feel heard tend to start hearing. It's like tuning a radio: you can't make the station clearer by turning up your own voice.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Accustom yourself to attend closely to what is said by others, and as far as possible to penetrate into the mind of the speaker.

Question: How do I respond to a bully?
Marcus Aurelius would say: See that you do not feel toward the inhuman as they feel toward their fellow men.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't let a cruel person turn you into a second cruel person. Protect yourself, and keep your own way of treating people. It's like being around someone with a heavy cold: the aim is to deal with them without catching what they have.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Look to it that you feel not towards the most inhuman of mankind, as they feel towards their fellows.

Question: How do I handle open hostility from a colleague or neighbour?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Does he hate me? Let him look to that. I will be mild and kind to all, and ready to show even him his mistake, without reproach.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If someone hates you, that is theirs to deal with. You stay mild and kind to everyone, and ready to show even that person their mistake, without scolding. It's like a shopkeeper with a rude customer: the same courtesy as for everyone else, because the courtesy belongs to the shopkeeper.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I shall be kind and good-natured to every one, and ready to shew his mistake to him that hates me; not in order to upbraid him, or to make a show of my patience, but from genuine goodness, like Phocion, if he indeed was sincere.

Question: How do I trust people after being hurt?
Marcus Aurelius would say: There is no need for suspicion where it is open to you to see what ought to be done. If you see your way, go on with goodwill.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You don't need suspicion when you can see what the right thing to do is. Work that out, and go forward in good faith. It's like driving again after an accident: you check your mirrors properly, and you don't treat every other car as an attacker.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): What need for suspicion when it is open for you to consider what ought to be done? If you see your way, proceed in it calmly, inflexibly. If you do not see it, pause and consult the best advisers.

Question: How do I stay myself around bad influences?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Like gold, or an emerald, or purple: whatever anyone does or says, keep your colour.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Whatever people around you do or say, keep your own colour, like gold or a gemstone. It's like stainless steel cutlery in a dishwasher full of other things: it comes out exactly as it went in.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is just as gold, or emeralds, or purple might say continually: “Let men do or say what they please, I must be an emerald, and retain my lustre”.

Question: How do I end a feud?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is a human being's special gift to love even those who err. They are kin, they err through ignorance, and soon both of you will be dead.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People who wrong you are your own kind, they act from ignorance, and soon you will both be gone. That is reason enough to end it. Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is man's special business to love even those who err; and to this love you attain, if it is borne in upon you that even these sinners are your kin, and that they offend through ignorance and against their will.

Question: What do I owe my parents?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He opens his book by recording what each gave him: from his father, modesty and manliness; from his mother, piety, generosity and simple living. Begin by naming the debt.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Start by naming the debt. He opened his notebook by writing down exactly what each parent gave him. It's like the credits at the end of a film: nothing gets made alone, and listing the names is the first way of saying thank you.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In the famous memory of my father I had a pattern of modesty and manliness.

Question: How can I be a better son or daughter?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask how you have behaved until now toward gods, parents, brothers, wife, children and teachers. Can it be said that you wronged none of them in deed or word?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Review your record plainly: how have you actually treated the people closest to you, in what you did and what you said? It's like reading your sent messages and not relying on memory: the record shows how you really spoke.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How have you behaved towards the Gods, towards your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who reared you, your friends, your intimates, your slaves?

Question: How do I deal with a difficult parent?

If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People are here for one another: help them do better, or bear with them. And expect the difficulty in advance, so it can't ambush you. It's like a house with a low doorway: you know it is there, so you duck and stop hitting your head.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Teach them better then, or bear with them.

Question: How do I get along with my brothers and sisters?

Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Of Severus, my brother, I learned to love my kinsmen, to love truth, to love justice. Through him I came to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, and Brutus. Question: How do I handle family arguments?
Marcus Aurelius would say: What does not profit the swarm does not profit the bee.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What is bad for the family as a whole can't be good for one member of it, even the one who "wins". It's like tackling your own teammate to get the ball: you came out on top, and your side still lost.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): What profits not the swarm profits not the bee.

Question: How do I care for ageing parents?

If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Being kind to the people who are yours is the proper work of a human being, and its own satisfaction. Do it without keeping a tally. It's like holding an umbrella over someone who once held one over you: you don't count the minutes.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): And his proper business is to be kindly to his fellows, to rise above the stirrings of sense, to be critical of every plausible imagination, and to contemplate universal Nature and all her consequences.

Question: Should I stay close to family who disapprove of my choices?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Adapt yourself to the life that has been given you, and truly love the people with whom it is your lot to live.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You don't choose the family you are given. Adapt to it, and love the people in it properly, even when they don't approve of you. It's like the seat you are allocated on a long flight: you can spend the journey resenting the neighbours, or get to know them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Adapt yourself to the things which your destiny has given you: love those with whom it is your lot to live, and love them with sincere affection.

Question: How do I accept my family as they are?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is fate that such actions come from such people. To want it otherwise is to want a fig tree without juice.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People act from what they are. Wanting your family to behave differently is wanting them to be other people. It's like expecting a cat to fetch: the disappointment is built in. Love the cat as a cat.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is fate that such actions should come from such men. He who would have it otherwise would have figs without juice. Question: How can I be grateful for my upbringing?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He thanked the gods for good grandparents, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good kinsmen and friends, and that he was never led to offend them.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He listed them: good grandparents, parents, sister, teachers and friends, and he counted it luck that he never badly wronged them. It's like the foundations of a house: you never see them, and every room you walk through stands on them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To the Gods I owe it that I had good grandfathers and parents, a good sister, good teachers, good servants, good kinsmen, and friends, good almost all of them.
