Question: What makes a good home?
Marcus Aurelius would say: In Sextus he saw a household governed with a father's affection, dignity without affectation, and patience with the ignorant.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A good home runs on affection, dignity without stiffness, and patience with people who don't know better. It's like a kitchen table: its worth is in who feels welcome to sit at it, not in what it cost.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Sextus was my pattern of a benign temper, and his family the model of a household governed by true paternal affection, and a steadfast purpose of living according to nature.

Question: How do I break a bad family pattern?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is ridiculous not to flee one's own faults, which is possible, and to try to flee other people's, which is not. Begin with the part that is yours.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Start with your own part, since that is the only part you can change. Running from other people's faults is impossible. It's like a chain letter that has gone round a family for generations: it stops with the first person who doesn't send it on.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is ridiculous that you flee not from the vice that is in yourself, as you have it in your power to do; but are still striving to flee from the vice in others, which you can never do.

Question: How do I balance my own life with my duty to family?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Everyone has three relations: to the body that surrounds him, to the divine cause from which all things come, and to those who live with him. Give each its due.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You have three sets of duties: to your own body and life, to what is greater than you, and to the people you live with. Give each its share. It's like a three-legged stool: shorten any one leg and it tips over.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): We have all of us three relations: the first to the manifold occasions of our state; the second to the supreme divine cause from which proceed all things unto all men; the third to those with whom we live.

Question: How do I forgive my parents?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Consider what they took to be good and evil when they acted. Seeing that, you will pity them and not be angry.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at what your parents believed was right when they acted. Seeing the mistaken idea behind it, you can feel pity where there was anger. It's like someone driving with an old, inaccurate map: they took the wrong road, and it was the only map they had.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whenever someone offends you, consider straightway how he has erred in his conceptions of good or evil. When you see where his error lies you will pity him, and be neither surprised nor angry.

Question: What did Marcus learn from his adoptive father?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Gentleness, constancy in decisions made after thought, no vanity about honours, love of work, and a ready ear for anyone with something for the common good.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Gentleness, sticking to a decision once it was properly thought through, no vanity about honours, love of work, and a ready ear for anyone with something useful to say. It's like an apprenticeship: he learned to rule the way a carpenter learns, by standing next to a master for years.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I learned from my father gentleness and undeviating constancy in judgments formed after due reflection; not to be puffed up with glory as men understand it; to be laborious and assiduous.

Question: How do I handle a family dispute over money or inheritance?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Never count as an advantage anything that will make you break faith or desert your honour.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Never count as a gain anything that costs you your word or your honour. It's like winning a board game at a family gathering by cheating: you get the win, and you lose the table.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Never esteem aught of advantage which will oblige you to break your faith, or to desert your honour; to hate, to suspect, or to execrate any man; to play a part; or to set your mind on anything that needs to be hidden by wall or curtain.

Question: How do I cope with being estranged from family?
Marcus Aurelius would say: A branch cut off can be grafted on again. But if the separation happens often, it becomes hard to grow together. Rejoin while it is possible.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A branch that has been cut off can be grafted back. But the more often it is cut, the harder the join. So reconnect while you still can. It's like a message left unanswered: the longer the silence, the heavier the reply becomes. Send it early.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): A branch cut off from its adjacent branch must necessarily be severed from the whole tree. Even so a man, parted from any fellow-man, has fallen away from the whole social community.

Question: What is the value of the wider family?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He records lessons from his grandfather, his great-grandfather, his mother, his brother and his adoptive father. He treated every relative as a teacher.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He treated every relative as a teacher, and wrote down a lesson from each. It's like a family group chat: easy to mute, and full of people who each know something you don't.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I owe it to my great-grandfather that I did not attend public lectures and discussions, but had good and able teachers at home; and I owe him also the knowledge that for things of this nature a man should count no expense too great.

Question: How do I honour a parent who has died?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do everything as a pupil of Antoninus: remember his constancy, his evenness, his sweetness, his contempt for empty fame.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Live as their pupil. Keep doing the things they did well: their steadiness, their kindness, their indifference to empty praise. It's like inheriting a toolbox: you honour it by using the tools, not by keeping it locked in the attic.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Imitate his resolute constancy to rational action, his level equability, his godliness, his serenity of countenance, his sweetness of temper, his contempt of vainglory, his keen attempts to comprehend things.

Question: How do I keep the peace with in-laws?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Attend closely to what is said, and look to the purpose behind what is done.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Listen carefully to what is actually said, and look for the purpose behind what is done. Most friction comes from guessing. It's like subtitles on a foreign film: read what was said before you decide what was meant.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In conversation we should give good heed to what is said, and in every enterprise we should attend to what is done. In the latter case, at once look to the end in view, and, in the former, note the meaning intended.

Question: How do I love my family without clinging to them?
Marcus Aurelius would say: When you kiss your child, whisper to yourself: tomorrow perhaps you will die. These are not words of bad omen. They name a work of nature.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Love them fully and remember, quietly, that nothing is guaranteed. There is nothing morbid in that. It is what makes the hug real. It's like a sunset: you watch it more closely because you know it won't stay.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Epictetus said that, when you kiss your child, you should whisper within yourself: “To-morrow perhaps he may die.” “Ill-omened words”! say you. “The words have no evil omen,”

Question: What does Marcus say about marriage?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Very little. He thanks the gods for a wife so obedient, so loving and so sincere. The rest must be drawn from what he says about living with other people.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He says very little about marriage: one line of thanks for a loving and sincere wife. The rest has to be drawn from what he says about living with people in general. It's like a cookbook with no chapter on breakfast: the same skills apply, and you work it out from the other recipes.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I must be grateful, too, that I have such a wife, so obedient, so loving, so ingenuous; that I had choice of fit and able men to whom I might commit the education of my children.

Question: How can I be a good partner?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Love those with whom it is your lot to live, and love them truly.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Love the person life has placed beside you, and mean it. It's like tending the garden you already have, and not spending your evenings browsing catalogues of other gardens.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Adapt yourself to the things which your destiny has given you: love those with whom it is your lot to live, and love them with sincere affection.

Question: How do I deal with arguments with my partner?

Question: How do I stop fearing that my partner will leave?

Question: How can I be single and content?

Question: How do I support a partner through a hard time?

Question: How do I disagree with my partner fairly?

Question: How do I recover from a divorce?

Question: Is it weak to depend on someone?

Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To my will the will of another is as indifferent as his poor breath and flesh. Question: What does he say about children?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He thanks the gods that his children were not dull or deformed, and that he found good teachers for them. He also faces, more than once, the thought of losing them.

Question: How do I raise good children?

Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I learned from my grandfather, Verus, to use good manners, and to put restraint on anger.

Question: How strict should I be with my children?

Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He taught me also to endure labour; not to need many things; to serve myself without troubling others; not to intermeddle in the affairs of others, and not easily to listen to slanders against them.

Question: How do I teach a child to be kind?

Question: How much should I spend on my child's education?

Question: How do I stop worrying about my children all the time?

Question: My friend is more successful than me and I envy them.
Marcus Aurelius would say: He may be better at this than you. He is not for that reason more public-spirited or more modest. And what profits the whole profits you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: They may be better at this than you. That doesn't make them a better person, and what is good for the group you both belong to is good for you too. It's like a teammate scoring: the goal goes on the same scoreboard as yours.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He is a better wrestler than you, but not more public-spirited, more modest, or better prepared for the accidents of fate; not more gentle toward the short-comings of his neighbours.

Question: How do I make friends as an adult?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Go from one unselfish act to another. Fellowship is built by acts, and each is its own reward.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't hunt for friends. Go from one useful, generous act to the next, and friendship forms around the doing. It's like joining a five-a-side team or a volunteer group: you turn up to do something together, and the friends are a by-product.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Find your sole delight and recreation in proceeding from one unselfish action to another, with God ever in mind.

Question: My friend and I disagree about politics. What then?
Marcus Aurelius would say: From Severus he took the idea of a state with equal laws and equal freedom of speech for all. Disagreement belongs to that freedom.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He admired the idea of a community with equal laws and free speech for everyone. Disagreement is part of that freedom, and no breach of it. It's like supporting rival football clubs: you can argue all match long and still share the drive home.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He gave me my first conception of a Commonwealth founded upon equitable laws and administered with equality of right; and of a Monarchy whose chief concern is the freedom of its subjects.

Question: I have lost touch with an old friend. Should I reach out?
Marcus Aurelius would say: How many who entered the world with me are already gone. Do it while you both can.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Many of the people you started out with are already gone. Contact them while you both can. It's like a library book you keep meaning to return: the longer you leave it, the harder it feels, and the fine was only ever in your head.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How many who entered the world with me are already departed!

Question: How do I tell a friend a hard truth?
Marcus Aurelius would say: With tact and without reproach, sincerely and not as a show of frankness.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Tell it with tact and without blame, and mean it for their good, never as a display of your own bluntness. It's like a good dentist: they tell you the truth about the tooth, and they are gentle while they do it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): But this must be done without irony or reproach, rather with loving-kindness and no bitterness of spirit; not as though you were reading him a lesson, or seeking admiration from any bystander, but as if you designed your remarks for him alone, though others may be present.

Question: My friend only calls when they need something.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Some people keep an account of every favour. Be the other kind: like the vine that bears its grapes and asks nothing.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Some people keep a ledger of every favour. Be the other sort: give the way a vine gives grapes, and move on. It's like a streetlight: it lights the way for whoever passes, and it never sends an invoice.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Some men, when they have done you a favour, are very ready to reckon up the obligation they have conferred. Others, again, are not so forward in their claims, but yet in their minds consider you their debtor, and well know the value of what they have done.

Question: How can I be a good listener?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Apply your mind to what is said, and enter into what is being done and why.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Give your full attention to what is being said, and try to understand what the person is doing and why. It's like putting your phone face down on the table: the first step of listening is showing that nothing else is competing.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Apply your mind to what is said. Penetrate all happenings and the causes thereof.

Question: Is it all right to outgrow friends?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Things that share a nature are drawn toward their own kind. The more a being reasons, the stronger the pull toward others like it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes. People are drawn toward those who share their nature, and that pull changes as you grow. It's like clothes from ten years ago: nothing is wrong with them, and they no longer fit. You can be grateful for them and still put them away.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): All things that share a common quality are strongly drawn to that which is of their own kind. The earthy tends towards the earth; fluids flow together, aerial bodies likewise; and naught but force prevents their confluence.

Question: How do I enjoy my friends more?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Take delight in their virtues: the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Deliberately notice what is admirable in each one: one's energy, another's modesty, a third's generosity. It's like eating a meal slowly: the food is the same as if you had bolted it, and you get far more from it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Consider the activity of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, and the other virtues of the rest. Nothing rejoices the heart so much as instances, the more the better, of goodness manifested in the characters of those around us.

Question: A friend betrayed me. How do I see friendship now?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Nothing is baser than a friendship of wolves: avoid it above all. The good and sincere person shows it in the eyes.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: One false friend shows you what to avoid: friendship that smiles and hides its teeth. It doesn't cancel the real kind, which shows plainly in a person's face. It's like one counterfeit banknote: it teaches you to check the watermark, and it doesn't make money worthless.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Nothing is baser than wolf-friendship. Shun it above all things. The good, straightforward, kindly man bears all these qualities in his eyes, and is not to be mistaken.

Question: How can I be a loyal friend?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Like Maximus: no one ever felt despised by him, and no one thought himself his better. He was cheerful, reliable, and did what was set before him without complaint.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be reliable and cheerful, and never make anyone feel small. Do what is in front of you without complaint. It's like a good old car: nothing flashy, and it starts every morning.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): No man could ever think himself despised by Maximus, and no one ever ventured to think himself his superior. He had also a good gift of humour.

Question: Do I need many friends?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He names about a dozen people who shaped him, and thanks the gods for them. A few who make one better are enough.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. He names around a dozen people who shaped him. A few who make you better are enough. It's like a bookshelf: a handful of books you reread do more for you than a wall of books you never open.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I give thanks that, having often been displeased with Rusticus, I never did anything to him which afterwards I might have had occasion to repent; that, though my mother was destined to die young, she lived with me all her latter years; that, as often as I inclined to succour any who were either poor or had fallen into some distress, I was never answered that there was not ready money enough to do it, and that I myself never had need of the like succour from another.

Question: How do I get motivated to work?
Marcus Aurelius would say: I am rising to the work of a human being. The plants, the birds, the ants, the bees all do their part. Shall I not do mine?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Remember what you are getting up for: the work of a human being. Everything in nature does its job, the plants, the birds, the ants, the bees. It's like a corner shop: the shutters go up and the bread is on the shelf because someone decided to turn up.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Do you not see the smallest plants, the little sparrows, the ants, the spiders, the bees, all doing their part, and working for order in the Universe, as far as in them lies?

Question: I hate my job. What should I do?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let no one hear you railing at the life of the court any more, and do not rail at it even to yourself.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stop complaining about the job, to others and inside your own head. The complaining makes the hours worse and changes nothing. It's like leaning on the horn in a traffic jam: the queue is the same length, and now it is loud.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Let no man any more hear you railing on the life of the court; nay, revile it not to your own hearing.

Question: How do I find work I love?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Those who love their craft wear themselves out at it, unwashed and unfed. Do you value your own nature less than the engraver values his engraving?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People who love their craft lose track of meals and sleep over it. Ask whether you value your own nature as much as a craftsman values his work. It's like a musician who practises for hours without being told: find the thing you would do without being chased.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Others, who love the art that they have made their own, exhaust themselves with labouring at it unwashed and unfed. But you honour your own nature less than the carver honours his carving, less than the dancer honours his dancing, the miser his gold, or the vain man his empty fame.

Question: How do I do good work?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do what falls to your hand with exact and unaffected dignity, with kindness, freedom and justice, as though it were the last act of your life.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Do whatever is in front of you with care and dignity, kindly and fairly, as if it were the last thing you would ever do. It's like a carpenter who sands the back of the drawer that nobody will see.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Hourly and earnestly strive, as a Roman and a man, to do what falls to your hand with perfect unaffected dignity, with kindliness, freedom and justice, and free your soul from every other imagination.

Question: How do I deal with a bad boss?
Marcus Aurelius would say: His character and his actions are his own. It is in your power to keep your own mind free from vice and disturbance. Do your part.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Your boss's character is your boss's. What stays in your power is keeping your own mind clear and doing your part well. It's like bad weather on a delivery round: you can't change the sky, and the parcels still get delivered properly.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Blot out false imaginations, and say often to yourself:—It is now in my power to preserve my soul free from all wickedness, all lust, all confusion or disturbance. And then, as I truly discern the nature of things, I can use them all in due proportion.

Question: How do I handle office politics?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Consider what such people are: whom they seek to please, what they hope to gain, and by what acts. Time will soon cover it all.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at what the players actually are: who they are trying to please, what they want, how they go about it. And remember how soon it will all be forgotten. It's like a reality show: gripping while it is on, and a year later nobody can name the contestants.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Consider what men are; whom they seek to please; what they expect to gain, and how they go about to compass their ends. Think how soon eternity will shroud all things, and how much is already shrouded.

Question: I was passed over for promotion. How do I cope?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Does this stop you from being just, generous, sober and wise? Then it has taken nothing that is yours.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask whether this stops you from being fair, generous, sensible and wise. If it doesn't, nothing that is truly yours has been taken. It's like the nameplate on an office door: they can change the plate, and your skills still walk out with you every evening.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be like a promontory against which the waves are always breaking. It stands fast, and stills the waters that rage around it. “Wretched am I,” says one, “that this has befallen me.”

Question: Should I change career?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask what is the soundest thing to do or say in this matter. Whatever it is, it is in your power to do it. Make no excuse of being hindered.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask what the soundest move is. Whatever it is, it is in your power to do, so don't hide behind "I can't". It's like standing at the edge of a swimming pool: the water doesn't get warmer the longer you think about it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In the present matter what is the soundest that can be done or said? For, whatever that may be, you are at liberty to do or say it. Make no excuses as if hindered. You will never cease from groaning until your disposition is such that what luxury is to men of pleasure, that to you is doing what is suitable to the constitution of man on every occasion that is thrown or falls in your way.

Question: How do I cope with boring work?
Marcus Aurelius would say: No work of hand or foot is against nature while it is the work of a hand or a foot. So no work is against a person's nature while it is a person's work.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No honest work is beneath a person, any more than walking is beneath a foot. It's like the washing-up after a good dinner: unglamorous, and part of what made the dinner possible.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): No toil for hand or foot is against Nature, so long as it is proper for hand or foot to do. No more, then, is toil contrary to the nature of man, as man, so long as he is doing work appointed for man to do; and if it be not contrary to his nature it cannot be evil for him.

Question: How do I balance work and the rest of life?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Love the art you have learned and find your rest in it. Spend the remainder of life as one who has entrusted everything to the gods.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Enjoy the craft you have learned and find your rest inside it, then leave the rest of life in larger hands. It's like a good meal: work is one dish on the table, and the meal is only right when the other dishes are there too.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Love the art which you have learned, humble though it be, and in it find your recreation. And spend the remainder of your life as one who with all his heart commits his concerns to the Gods, and neither acts the tyrant nor the slave to any of mankind.

Question: How do I deal with a colleague who does not pull their weight?
Marcus Aurelius would say: I do my duty. Other things do not distract me.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Do your own job and don't let their behaviour distract you from it. It's like running your leg of a relay: you can't run theirs for them, and you can run yours flat out.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I do my duty, and for the rest am not distracted by anything which is inanimate or irrational, or which has lost or ignores the proper way.

Question: Someone took credit for my work.
Marcus Aurelius would say: When you have done a kind act and another has benefited, why look for a third thing: to be seen to have done it?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You did something good and someone benefited. Wanting a third thing, to be seen doing it, is the part that makes you miserable. It's like planting a tree in a public park: the shade is there for everyone, with or without a plaque.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): When you have done a kind action, another has benefited. Why do you, like the fools, require some third thing in addition—a reputation for benevolence or a return for it.

Question: How do I ask for help at work?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Without shame. A soldier who cannot scale the wall alone climbs with another's help.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Without embarrassment. The job is to get the work done, not to get it done alone, and asking early is a kindness to everyone who depends on the result. It's like asking a taller colleague to reach the top shelf: nobody thinks less of you, and the thing gets reached.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): What, then, if you are lame, and cannot scale the battlements alone, but can with another's help?

Question: Am I up to this job?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Is my understanding sufficient for this or not? If it is, I use it as a tool given by nature. If not, I yield to one who can do it better, or do what I can with a helper.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask it plainly. If your ability is enough, use it. If it isn't, hand the job to someone better, or do your share with their help. It's like checking the weight limit on a ladder before you climb: knowing the answer is how the job gets done safely.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If it be sufficient, I use it for the work in hand as an instrument given to me by nature. If it be not sufficient, I either give place to one better fitted for the achievement, or, if for some reason this be not a proper course, I do it as best I can, taking the aid of those who, by directing my mind, can accomplish something fit and serviceable for the common good.

Question: How do I cope with being made redundant?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You are a part of the whole, and what the whole brings is no injury to the part. Then order life again, one act at a time.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You are one part of a much larger whole, and what the whole goes through is no personal attack on the part. Then rebuild, one step at a time. It's like a shop closing when a town's trade shifts: it is the economy moving, and no verdict on the person behind the counter.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whether all be atoms, or there be a universal Law of Nature, let it be laid down first that I am a part of the whole which is governed by Nature; secondly, that I am associated with other parts like myself.

Question: How do I stay ethical under pressure at work?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If it is not fitting, do not do it. If it is not true, do not say it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Use a two-line test: if it isn't right, don't do it. If it isn't true, don't say it. It's like the red line on a rev counter: you don't debate with it each time. You just don't cross it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If a thing be not becoming, do it not; if not true, say it not.

Question: How should I speak at work?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Speak, in the Senate or anywhere, with dignity more than elegance, and let your words be sound.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Speak with substance and dignity, and don't worry about sounding impressive. People act on what they understand, so say the true thing in plain words. It's like the signs in an airport: clear beats clever, every time.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Speak, whether in the Senate or elsewhere, with dignity rather than elegance; and let your words ever be sound and virtuous.

Question: I have retired. What is my purpose now?
Marcus Aurelius would say: What is to be valued? Not applause. To move and to hold oneself according to one's own constitution, as every craft aims at making its product fit for its work.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The applause was never the point. What matters is still available: living and acting in line with what you are built for. It's like a retired teacher who starts mentoring: the classroom is gone, and the thing they were good at is still there to be used.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): This is the end of all arts and studies, for every art aims at making what it produces well adapted to the work for which it was designed. The gardener, the vine-dresser, the horse-breaker, the dog-trainer all try for this; and what else is the aim of all education and teaching?

Question: How do I keep high standards without perfectionism?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not hope for Plato's Republic. Be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and count that as no small result.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't wait for the ideal. If one small thing moves forward, count that as real progress. It's like software: version one ships with flaws, and it is worth more than the perfect version that never leaves the laptop.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Set about it if you have the means; and look not around you to see if any be taking notice, neither hope to realize Plato's Republic. Be satisfied if the smallest thing go well.

Question: How do I cope with work that goes unnoticed?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Like the vine that has borne grapes, the horse that has run, the bee that has made honey: go on to the next thing without calling out.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Do the work and move on to the next piece without announcing it, like a vine that has produced its grapes. It's like the people who maintain the water supply: you only think of them when it fails, and they are the reason your tap works every morning.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The horse when he has run his course, the hound when he has followed the track, the bee when it has made its honey, and the man when he has done good to others, make no noisy boast of it, but set out to do the same once more, as the vine in its season produces its new clusters again.

Question: What makes a good leader?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Antoninus: gentle, immovable once a thing was weighed, without vanity, hard-working, open to anyone with something for the common good, and just to every person.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: His model was his adoptive father: gentle, firm once a matter had been properly weighed, free of vanity, hard-working, open to anyone with a useful idea, and fair to each person. It's like a good ship's captain: a calm voice, a clear course, and the crew's welfare before their own comfort.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He taught me to give ready hearing to any man who offered anything tending to the common good; to mete out impartial justice to every one; to apprehend rightly when severity and when clemency should be used; to abstain from all impure lusts; and to use humanity towards all men.

Question: How do I avoid letting power change me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: See that you do not fall into Caesarism. Guard your simplicity, your goodness, your sincerity, your dignity, your love of justice and your kindness.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Watch that the role doesn't soak into you. Keep your simplicity, goodness, sincerity, sense of justice and kindness. It's like a stage costume: wear it for the performance, and take it off before you go home, or one day you can't.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Guard your simplicity, your goodness, your sincerity, your dignity, your reticence, your love of justice, your piety, your kindliness, your affection for your kin, and your constancy to your duty.

Question: How do I make decisions for a team?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do only what the ruling and lawmaking reason suggests for the good of people. And be ready to change course if someone can set you right.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Decide on what serves the people affected, and stay ready to change course when someone shows you a better way. It's like a head chef who writes the menu and still tastes what the junior cook suggests.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): For two things be ever ready: First, to do that only which reason, the sovereign and legislative faculty, suggests for the good of mankind: Secondly, to change your course on meeting any one who can correct and alter your opinion.

Question: How do I lead people who resist?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Try to persuade them. But pursue the course you have marked out when the principles of justice point that way, whether they agree or not.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Try persuasion first. If what is right is clear, keep to the course whether or not they come round. It's like a doctor with a reluctant patient: explain patiently, and don't change the prescription to win a smile.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Try to persuade men to agree with you; but whether they agree or not, pursue the course you have marked out when the principles of justice point that way. Should one oppose you by force, act with resignation, and shew not that you are hurt, use the obstruction for the exercise of some other virtue, and remember that your purpose involved the reservation that you were not to aim at impossibilities.

Question: How do I handle criticism as a leader?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If the sailors revile their pilot, or the sick their physician, whom else will they follow? Keep to the task of bringing them safely through.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People complain about whoever is steering. If the crew curses the pilot, who else will they follow? Keep to the task of getting them through safely. It's like a mountain guide: the group moans about the pace, and the guide's job is still to get everyone down before dark.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If the sailors revile their pilot, or the sick their physician, whom will they follow or obey? And how will the one secure safety to the crew, or the other health to the patients?

Question: How do I delegate well?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Antoninus gave way without envy to those with a special gift, in speaking, in law or in anything else, and helped each to be honoured for it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Give way, without envy, to whoever is best at the thing, and help them get the credit for it. It's like a football manager: you don't take the penalties yourself. You pick the best penalty taker, and you cheer.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It was his special merit to yield without envy to any who had acquired any special faculty, as either eloquence, or learning in the Law, in ancient customs, or the like; and he aided such men strenuously, so that every one of them might be regarded and esteemed for his special excellence.

Question: How do I stay humble at the top?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Hold to the idea he took from Severus: a state with equal laws for all, equal rights and free speech, and a rule that honours above all the freedom of the governed.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Hold on to the principle of equal rules for everyone, free speech, and respect for the freedom of the people you lead. It's like a head chef who eats the same staff meal as everyone else: the rules of the kitchen apply to the person who wrote them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He gave me my first conception of a Commonwealth founded upon equitable laws and administered with equality of right; and of a Monarchy whose chief concern is the freedom of its subjects.

Question: How do I serve the people I lead?
Marcus Aurelius would say: What does not profit the swarm does not profit the bee. Have I done something for the common good? Then I have had my advantage.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What doesn't help the group can't help you. If you did something for the common good, you have already been paid. It's like the lift in a shared building: if it breaks, it doesn't matter which floor is yours.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): What profits not the swarm profits not the bee.

Question: How do I handle the loneliness of leadership?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Live as on a mountain. It makes no difference whether one is here or there, if one lives everywhere as a citizen of the world.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stand apart if you must, as on a mountain, and remember that you belong to the wider world wherever you are. It's like the night watch on a ship: quiet and solitary, and everyone asleep below is the reason you are there.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): For it makes no difference whether we live here or there, provided we live like citizens everywhere in the world. Let men see and know you as a man indeed, living according to Nature.

Question: How do I make unpopular decisions?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is the part of a king to do good and reap reproach.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Doing good and being criticised for it comes with the role. It's like a team doctor who rests a star player before a final: the right call, and the least popular one in the room.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It is a saying of Antisthenes, that it is the part of a king to do good and reap reproach.

Question: How should I manage money that is not mine?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Antoninus was ever watchful of the needs of the empire, a careful steward of the public revenue, and tolerant of the criticism this brought him.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be a careful steward: watch what is truly needed, spend other people's money carefully, and accept the grumbling that brings. It's like looking after a friend's house while they are away: you don't redecorate it to your own taste.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Ever watchful of the needs of the Empire, a careful steward of the public revenue, he was tolerant of the censure of others in affairs of that kind. He was neither a superstitious worshipper of the Gods, nor an ambitious pleaser of men, nor studious of popularity, but in all things sober and steadfast, well skilled in what was honourable, never affecting novelties.

Question: How do I handle flattery?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He checked applause and every kind of flattery around him.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Shut it down. His adoptive father stopped applause and flattery around him. It's like sugar: pleasant in the moment, and a steady diet of it rots the judgement.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I observed his zeal to retain his friends without being fickle or over fond; his contentment in every condition; his cheerfulness; his forethought about very distant events; his unostentatious attention to the smallest details; his restraint of all popular applause and flattery.

Question: How do I stay calm in a crisis as a leader?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Like Maximus: master of himself, never hurried, never hesitant, never at a loss. Cheerful in illness as in every other circumstance.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be master of yourself: unhurried, never dithering, never lost, and in good humour whatever the circumstances. It's like an emergency-room doctor: the room is chaos, and the calmest person in it is the one in charge.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The counsels of Maximus taught me to command myself, to judge clearly, to be of good courage in sickness and other misfortunes, to be moderate, gentle, yet serious in disposition, and to accomplish my appointed task without repining.

Question: How do I give instructions well?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do steadily what human nature requires, and say what seems most just, yet with kindliness, modesty and sincerity.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Do what the situation requires, and say what is fair, with kindness, modesty and sincerity. It's like good assembly instructions for furniture: clear steps, no showing off, and nobody made to feel stupid.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Do unflinchingly whatever man's nature requires, and speak as seems most just, yet in kindliness, modesty, and sincerity.

Question: How do I judge people fairly?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Enter into the governing mind of others, and let others enter into your own.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Make the effort to understand how each person thinks, and let them see how you think. It's like a job interview that runs both ways: nobody can be judged fairly from a CV alone.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Penetrate into the governing part of others; and also allow others to enter into your own.

Question: How do I keep going when leading feels thankless?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Wish for one thing only: to act or to refrain as the reason of the community requires.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Want only one thing: to act, or hold back, as the good of the group requires. Thanks are a bonus. It's like a goalkeeper: remembered for the one mistake, rarely for the many saves, and still diving for every ball.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Wish for one thing only; always to act or to refrain as social wisdom requires.

Question: How do I build a team that works together?
Marcus Aurelius would say: We are made for cooperation, like the feet, the hands, the eyelids, the upper and lower rows of teeth.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People are built for cooperation, like two hands or two rows of teeth. Build the team so that each part needs the other. It's like an orchestra: nobody plays every instrument, and the music exists only when they play together.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I cannot be angry with my brother, or sever myself from him, for we are made by nature for mutual assistance, like the feet, the hands, the eyelids, the upper and lower rows of teeth.

Question: How do I deal with someone who is underperforming?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If he is going wrong, instruct him kindly and show him his mistake. If you cannot, blame yourself, or blame no one.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Show them kindly where they are going wrong. If you can't get through, look first at how you explained it, or blame nobody. It's like a good coach reviewing match footage with a player: here is what happened, and here is what to try next.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If a man is going wrong, instruct him kindly, and shew him his mistake. If you are unable to do this, blame yourself or none.

Question: How do I plan ahead and still act today?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Antoninus looked far ahead at distant events and attended to the smallest details without show.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look a long way ahead and handle the small details, without making a show of either. It's like a chess player: thinking several moves on, and still making only the one move that is due now.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): I observed his zeal to retain his friends without being fickle or over fond; his contentment in every condition; his cheerfulness; his forethought about very distant events; his unostentatious attention to the smallest details; his restraint of all popular applause and flattery.

Question: How should a leader take advice?
Marcus Aurelius would say: To change course and follow one who can set you right is no loss of freedom. The act is still yours.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Changing course because someone showed you a better way costs you no freedom. The decision is still yours. It's like a surgeon asking for a second opinion: it is one of the signs of a good surgeon.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember that to change your course, and to follow any man who can set you right is no compromise of your freedom. The act is your own, performed on your own impulse and judgment, and according to your own understanding.

Question: What does Marcus say about money?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Little directly. He treats wealth as a thing indifferent: to be used without pride when present and not missed when absent.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He says little directly. He treats wealth as neither good nor bad: use it without pride when you have it, and don't ache for it when you don't. It's like an umbrella: handy when it is there, and not worth grieving over when it is left on the train.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As to the things which make the ease of life, and which fortune can supply in such abundance, he used them without pride, and yet with all freedom: enjoyed them without affectation when they were present, and when absent he found no want of them.

Question: How much is enough?
Marcus Aurelius would say: His mother taught him to live with a simplicity far from what is usual among the rich. Enough is what serves a plain life.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Enough is what a plain life actually needs. He was raised to live far more simply than his family's wealth allowed. It's like a buffet: the right amount is what you can enjoy, not what you can pile on the plate.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Of my mother I learned to be pious and generous; to keep myself not only from evil deeds, but even from evil thoughts; and to live with a simplicity which is far from customary among the rich.

Question: How do I stop wanting more things?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look at what things are made of: this purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shellfish. Strip them of the words that make them grand.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at what the thing is made of, without the brand story. His example was a prestige robe: sheep's wool, dyed with shellfish. It's like an expensive trainer: rubber, fabric and glue, plus a logo. See the materials, and the wanting cools.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Think of your purple robes as sheep's wool stained in the blood of a shell-fish. Such conceptions, which touch reality so near, and set forth the sum and substance of these objects, are powerful indeed to display to us their despicable value.

Question: How do I cope with financial stress?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Stay with the first report: this bill is due. Do not add "I am ruined". Then take the next necessary act. This is perspective, and not financial advice.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stay with the plain fact: this bill is due. Don't add "I am finished". Then do the next necessary thing, such as one phone call or one list. It's like untangling headphones: you don't pull at the whole knot. You free one loop at a time. This is perspective, and not financial advice.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Dwell thus upon first appearances; add nothing to them from within, and no harm befalls you: or rather add the recognition that all is part of the world's lot.

Question: Is it wrong to be rich?
Marcus Aurelius would say: No. Antoninus used the comforts fortune supplied in plenty, without pride and without apology. When they were absent he did not want them.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. His adoptive father enjoyed the comforts he had, without pride and without apology, and didn't miss them when they were absent. It's like a guest at a generous table: you enjoy the meal, and you would be the same person at a simpler one.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As to the things which make the ease of life, and which fortune can supply in such abundance, he used them without pride, and yet with all freedom: enjoyed them without affectation when they were present, and when absent he found no want of them.

Question: How do I deal with envy of wealthy people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Judge the worth of what most people call goods from this: one can hear the joke about the rich man who has so much he has nowhere left to relieve himself, and find it fitting.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at how much trouble great wealth brings with it, and how easily the man with too much becomes a joke. It's like a house with ten bedrooms for two people: more to clean, more to guard, and still only one bed to sleep in.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Of what value the things are which the many account good you may judge from this: If a man has conceived certain things, such as prudence, temperance, justice, or courage, to be good in the real sense, he cannot, while he is of this mind, readily listen to the traditional gibe about a superabundance of good things.

Question: I lost a lot of money. How should I see it?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Receive the gifts of fortune without pride, and part with them without reluctance.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What fortune gave, fortune took back. Accept the first without swagger and the second without clinging. It's like a seat on a busy train: you had it for a few stops, and it was never yours to keep.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Receive the gifts of fortune without pride; and part with them without reluctance.

Question: Should I lend or give money to friends and family?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Help the one who needs it, according to your power and his desert. He was thankful that when he wished to help someone in need, he had the means.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Help the person in need as far as your means and their situation warrant. He was grateful simply to have the means when he wanted to help. It's like lending a ladder to a neighbour: lend what you could bear not to get back, and you will never resent it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be not incautiously carried away by sentiment, but aid him that needs it according to your power and his desert. If his need be of the things which are indifferent, think not that he is harmed thereby, for so to think is an evil habit.

Question: How should I think about debt?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He gives no rule. His tests apply: is this necessary, and shall I regret it? Take professional advice on the numbers.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He gives no rule on debt. His general tests still apply: is this necessary, and will I regret it? It's like taking on a pet: the question isn't only the cost on day one. It is whether you can carry what follows. For the actual numbers, take professional advice.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): This is perhaps a better saying, “Do what is necessary, do what the reason of the being that is social in its nature directs, and do it in the spirit of that direction.” By this you will attain the calm that comes from virtuous action, and that calm also which comes from having few things to do.

Question: How can I be generous?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do good as the vine bears grapes: without looking for anything in return.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Give the way a vine gives grapes: produce the good, and don't look round for the return. It's like leaving a good book on a train seat for the next passenger: no name, no thanks, and the pleasure is in the leaving.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The horse when he has run his course, the hound when he has followed the track, the bee when it has made its honey, and the man when he has done good to others, make no noisy boast of it, but set out to do the same once more, as the vine in its season produces its new clusters again.

Question: Does money buy happiness?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He says of his own search that happiness was not found in wealth, or in fame, or in pleasure. It is in doing what human nature requires.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He tried the usual candidates himself, and reports that happiness wasn't in wealth, fame or pleasure. It is in doing what a human being is built to do. It's like a bigger television: the picture is sharper for a week, and then it is just your television.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You have made many efforts and wandered much, but you have nowhere found happiness; not in syllogisms, not in riches, not in fame or pleasure, not in anything. Where, then, is it?

Question: How do I stop comparing my income with other people's?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Much leisure is gained by the one who does not look at what his neighbour says or does or intends.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stop looking at what the neighbour earns, says or plans. You gain a great deal of peace and time. It's like reading someone else's fuel gauge while you drive: it tells you nothing about how far your own car will go.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How much he gains in leisure who looks not to what his neighbours say, or do, or intend; but considers only how his own actions may be just and holy, looking not, as Agathon says, to the moral example of others, but running a straight course and never turning therefrom.

Question: How should I handle sudden wealth?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Receive it without pride, and guard your simplicity.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Take it without pride, and keep living simply. It's like being handed a microphone: it makes you louder, not wiser, so stay the person you were before the volume went up.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Receive the gifts of fortune without pride; and part with them without reluctance.

Question: Is it bad to want to be wealthy?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The pleasure-seeker places his good in his own sensations, and the lover of fame in what others do. The person of understanding places it in his own actions.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Wanting wealth isn't the problem. Placing your happiness in it is, because then your good depends on things outside you. Place it in your own actions. It's like a boat: fine while the boat is in the water, and a problem once the water is in the boat.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The vain-glorious man places his happiness in the action of others. The sensualist finds it in his own sensations. The wise man realizes it in his own work.

Question: How do I live simply?
Marcus Aurelius would say: As he was shown young: the philosopher's plank bed and skins, needing little, and doing things for himself.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Need little and do things for yourself. He was shown this young: a hard bed and plain habits. It's like a kitchen with five good tools in place of fifty gadgets: easier to use, and nothing to dig through.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Him also I must thank for my hearing first Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus; that I wrote dialogues in my youth, and took a liking to the philosopher's pallet and skins, and to the other things which, by the Grecian discipline, belong to that profession.

Question: Should I buy this expensive thing?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask whether it is one of the necessary things. And look at what it is made of.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask two things: is it necessary, and what is it actually made of once the branding is stripped off? It's like leaving an item in an online basket overnight: by morning the wanting has often gone, and the answer is clear.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): This is perhaps a better saying, “Do what is necessary, do what the reason of the being that is social in its nature directs, and do it in the spirit of that direction.” By this you will attain the calm that comes from virtuous action, and that calm also which comes from having few things to do.

Question: How do I teach my children about money?
Marcus Aurelius would say: By living plainly yourself. He learned simplicity by watching his mother and his tutor.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: By living plainly yourself. He learned simplicity by watching his mother and his tutor, not from lectures. It's like table manners: children copy the hands they see at dinner.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Of my mother I learned to be pious and generous; to keep myself not only from evil deeds, but even from evil thoughts; and to live with a simplicity which is far from customary among the rich.

Question: What should I make of luxury and status symbols?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Marble is hardened earth. Gold and silver are its dregs. A robe is animal hair, and purple dye is blood.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: See them as their raw materials. Marble is hardened earth, gold is sediment, fine cloth is animal hair. It's like a diamond: carbon, the same element as the tip of a pencil.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Again; marble is but the concrete humour of the earth, gold and silver its heavy dregs. Our garments are but hair, the purple dye blood. All else is of a like nature. Breath, too, is just the same, ever changing from this to that.

Question: How do I deal with the fear of being poor?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Remember the country mouse and the town mouse, and the fear and trembling of the town mouse.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Remember the fable of the country mouse and the town mouse: the rich table came with constant fear. A plainer life holds less to be afraid of. It's like a driver with nothing valuable in the car: they park anywhere and sleep well.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember the country mouse and the town mouse; and how the latter feared and trembled.

Question: Should I invest in this or take this financial risk?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He gives no rule for this. His test for any act is whether you will regret it and whether it suits a reasonable, social being. Take professional advice for the rest.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He gives no rule for investing. His test for any act is whether you will regret it and whether it fits a sensible person with duties to others. It's like deciding whether to climb in doubtful weather: ask what you can afford to lose, and who depends on you. For the rest, take professional advice.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): What more should I desire if my present action is becoming to an intelligent and a social being, subject to the same law with Gods?

Question: Is ambition a bad thing?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ambition that places its good in what other people do is a kind of slavery. Place it in your own acts.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: It depends where it aims. Ambition that needs other people's applause makes you their servant. Aim it at your own actions. It's like running to beat your own best time and not for the crowd: that is a race you can win every day.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The vain-glorious man places his happiness in the action of others. The sensualist finds it in his own sensations. The wise man realizes it in his own work.

Question: How should I define success?
Marcus Aurelius would say: To make one's fortune is to give oneself good things, and the true good things are a worthy frame of mind, worthy impulses and worthy actions.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Success is giving yourself the real goods: a sound mind, sound motives, sound actions. It's like a house: the valuation that matters is whether it is good to live in, not the figure in the estate agent's window.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In whatever case I had been left I could have made my fortune: for what is it to make a fortune but to confer good things upon one's self; and true good things are a worthy frame of mind, worthy impulses, worthy actions.

Question: I want to be famous. Is it worth it?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The familiar names of old are now strange, and those once sung are forgotten. What then is worth effort? Just thoughts, unselfish acts, and speech that never lies.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The famous names of the past are fading words now. What is worth the effort is fair thinking, useful acts and truthful speech. It's like the music charts from twenty years ago: songs that everyone knew, and most people couldn't hum them today.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The familiar phrases of old days are now strange and obsolete; and, likewise, the names of such as were once much celebrated now sound strangely in our ears. Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus; after them Scipio and Cato; lastly, Augustus, Hadrian, and Antonine—all are forgotten.

Question: How do I keep going without recognition?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Have I done something for the common good? Then I have had my advantage.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If what you did was useful to others, you have already been paid. It's like the person who wrote the code inside an app that many people use: no one knows the name, and the thing works.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Have I done anything for the common good? Is not this itself my advantage? Let this thought be ever with you, and desist not.

Question: I feel behind in life. What would he say?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It is no longer in your power to have lived your whole life as you wished. Leave reputation aside, and be content to live the rest as nature wills.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You can't go back and live the earlier years differently. Drop the scoreboard, and live the rest the way a person is meant to. It's like joining a walk halfway along the trail: the view from here on is exactly as good.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Now therefore, as you see how the matter truly lies, put from you all thoughts of reputation among men; and let it suffice you to live so long as your nature wills, though that be but the scanty remnant of a life.

Question: How do I stay grounded after a success?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Rejoice in simplicity and modesty, and be indifferent to what lies between virtue and vice.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Enjoy simplicity and modesty, and stay unimpressed by everything that isn't a matter of character. It's like an athlete the morning after a final: the medal is in a drawer, and training starts at the usual time.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Rejoice yourself with simplicity, modesty, and indifference to all things that lie between good and bad. Love mankind, and obey God. “All things,” says someone, “go by law and order.”

Question: What legacy should I aim for?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Those who will remember you will themselves soon die. Secure the benefit of the present time.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The people who will remember you will also be gone soon. Put your effort into the good you can do now. It's like growing vegetables where you could have carved your name on a tree: one of them feeds people this season.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He who is careful and troubled about the fame which is to live after him considers not that each one of those who remember him must very soon die himself, and thereafter also the succeeding generation, until every memory of him, handed on by excited and ephemeral admirers, dies utterly away.

Question: Is competing with others healthy?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Compete in what counts: to be more public-spirited, more modest, better prepared for what happens, and gentler with a neighbour's faults.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes, if you compete on the right things: being more useful, more modest, readier for whatever comes, and more patient with other people's faults. It's like a race in which every runner can win at once.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He is a better wrestler than you, but not more public-spirited, more modest, or better prepared for the accidents of fate; not more gentle toward the short-comings of his neighbours.

Question: How do I handle a rival?
Marcus Aurelius would say: We show no resentment toward a sparring partner. Keep out of the way of his blows, without suspicion or hatred.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Treat a rival like a sparring partner: avoid the blows, hold no grudge, and let them sharpen you. It's like two coffee shops on the same street: each one's good coffee forces the other to get better.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As I said, we may keep out of their way, but without suspicion or hatred.

Question: Why am I never satisfied with what I achieve?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The spider is proud of catching a fly, one man of a hare, another of a boar, another of prisoners of war. Look at the principle and they are all alike.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Every catch feels grand to the one who made it, and it is all the same chase. Seeing that lets you step off the wheel. It's like the levels in a game: each one promises that the next will be the one that satisfies, and there is always another.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The spider exults when he has captured a fly; one man because he has taken a little hare, another because he has netted an anchovy, another because he has hunted down a wild boar or a bear; and another because he has conquered the Sarmatians.

Question: How do I pursue a big goal without being crushed if it fails?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Set out with a reservation. If the way is blocked, the mind makes material of the block, as a fire masters what falls on it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Go after it with a condition attached: "if nothing prevents it". Then, if the way closes, you turn the obstacle into your next material, the way a fire uses what is thrown on it. It's like a climber who sets out for the summit and also plans the descent: the aim is fixed, and the grip on it is loose.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): It requires no set material to work upon, but, under proper reservation, needs but the incitement to pursue, and makes matter for its activities out of every opposition. Even so a fire masters that which is cast upon it, and though a small flame would have been extinguished, your great blaze quickly makes the added fuel its own, consumes it, and grows mightier therefrom.

Question: What is worth striving for?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If you find anything better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, turn to it with all your heart. If not, give place to nothing else.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Justice, truth, self-control and courage. If you ever find something better, give it everything. If not, let nothing else take first place. It's like a compass: it doesn't tell you the weather, and it always tells you the direction.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If in the life of man you find anything better than justice, truth, sobriety, manliness; and, in sum, anything better than the satisfaction of your soul with itself in that wherein it is given to you to follow right reason; and with fate in that which is determined beyond your control; if, I say, you find aught better than this, then turn thereto with all your heart, and enjoy it as the best that is to be found.

Question: How do I feel about other people's success?
Marcus Aurelius would say: All that happens to the individual profits the whole. What profits the whole profits each part.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Their win is a win for the whole you belong to, and what helps the whole helps you. It's like a new shop doing well on your street: more people come, and every shopfront benefits.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): All that happens to the individual is of profit to the whole. This would suffice. But if you consider closely you will see that it is also a general truth that all that happens to one man is of profit to the rest of mankind.

Question: Should I care how I will be remembered?
Marcus Aurelius would say: People will not praise those who live with them, yet they set great store by the praise of posterity, whom they have never seen.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: It is odd: people ignore the opinion of those around them and long for the praise of future strangers they will never meet. It's like dressing up for a party you will not be attending.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): They can speak no good word of the contemporaries with whom they live; yet they count it a great thing to gain the praises of a posterity whom they never saw nor shall see.

Question: How do I deal with the fear of being ordinary?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Asia and Europe are corners of the universe. The whole sea is a drop. All present time is a point.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Step back far enough and every life is small: continents are corners, the ocean is a drop, the present is a point. Ordinary and famous look the same from there. It's like a city seen from a plane at night: every window is one small light, the mansion's and the flat's alike.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Asia and Europe are mere corners of the Universe: the whole sea is but a drop, Athos a clod. All the present is but an instant in eternity. All things are small, changeable, and fleeting.

Question: How do I stay driven and still be content?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Be satisfied with your present opinion if it is certain, your present action if it is social, and your present temper if it is content with what comes.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be content with three things: that your present view is well founded, your present action is useful to others, and your present mood accepts what comes. The drive belongs in the action. It's like a keen hiker: walking hard, and enjoying the path they are on.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be satisfied with your present opinion, if certain; with your present course of action, if social; with your present mood, if well pleased with all that comes upon you from without.

Question: Is it wrong to want to be the best?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Aim to be the best at what is fully yours: sincerity, dignity, endurance, kindness, contentment. No one can stop you there.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Not if you pick the right contest. Aim to be the best at what is fully yours: sincerity, dignity, stamina, kindness, contentment. It's like being the most reliable person on a team: nobody else has to lose for you to hold that title.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be sincere, be dignified, be painstaking; scorn pleasure, repine not at fate, need little; be kind and frank; love not exaggeration and vain talk; strive after greatness.

Question: What happens after the peak of a career?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Recall the age of Vespasian: people marrying, raising children, scheming, wanting high office. That whole life is nowhere now.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at any earlier generation: marrying, raising children, scheming, chasing office. All of it is gone. The peak was never the point. It's like an old stadium: the crowd that roared there has gone home, and what was worth having was the playing.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Recall, for example, the age of Vespasian. It is as the spectacle of our own time. You will see men marrying, bringing up children, sick and dying, warring and feasting, trading and farming.

Question: What is the point of achievement?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The joy of a human being is to do the proper work of a human being.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The point is the doing: a human being's joy is doing the proper work of a human being. It's like cooking a meal: the pleasure is in making it and sharing it, not in the photograph of the plate.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The joy of man is to do his proper business. And his proper business is to be kindly to his fellows, to rise above the stirrings of sense, to be critical of every plausible imagination, and to contemplate universal Nature and all her consequences.

Question: How do I choose between money and meaning?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Never esteem as an advantage anything that will oblige you to break your faith or desert your honour.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Never count as a gain anything that costs you your word or your honour. Inside that line, choose freely. It's like the guardrail on a mountain road: it doesn't choose your destination. It marks the edge you don't go over.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Never esteem aught of advantage which will oblige you to break your faith, or to desert your honour; to hate, to suspect, or to execrate any man; to play a part; or to set your mind on anything that needs to be hidden by wall or curtain.

Question: How do I recover from failure?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not fret, despond or lose heart. When driven off course, come back, and be glad if most of your acts are worthy of a human being.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't sulk or lose heart. When you are knocked off course, come back, and be glad if most of what you do is decent. It's like a toddler learning to walk: they fall again and again, and nobody calls it failure. They call it learning.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Fret not, neither despond nor be disheartened, if it be not always possible for you to act according to your principles of perfection. If you are beaten off, return again to the effort, and content yourself that your conduct is generally such as becomes a man.

Question: I made a terrible mistake. What now?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Then change. To follow one who can set you right is no disgrace.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Then change. Being corrected and following a better course is nothing to be ashamed of. It's like taking a wrong turn while driving: the mistake costs a few minutes. Refusing to turn round costs the whole journey.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember that to change your course, and to follow any man who can set you right is no compromise of your freedom. The act is your own, performed on your own impulse and judgment, and according to your own understanding.

Question: How do I stop regretting the past?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Regret is a self-reproach for having neglected something useful. Take what is useful from it and act.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Regret points at something useful you neglected. Take the useful part and act on it. It's like the receipt for an expensive lesson: keep what you learned, and stop rereading the price.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Repentance is a self-reproving, because we have neglected something useful. Whatever is good must be useful in some sort, and worthy of the care of a good and honourable man.

Question: I feel like I have wasted my life.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Consider yourself as dead and your life as finished. Live what remains as a gift, according to nature.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Treat the old life as finished. Whatever time remains is a gift on top, and you can live it well from today. It's like the second half of a match after a poor first half: the earlier score stands, and the rest of the game is still to be played.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Consider yourself as dead, your life as finished and past. Live what yet remains according to Nature's laws, as an overplus granted to you beyond your hope.

Question: Is it too late for me to change?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You have seen the other state. Make trial of this one too. Avoid perplexity and seek simplicity.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. You have seen what the old way gives you. Try the other way, and keep it simple. It's like a book you put down years ago: the bookmark is where you left it, and you can pick it up tonight.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You have seen the other state, make trial also of this. Avoid perplexity; seek simplicity. Has a man sinned? He bears his own sin. Has aught befallen you? It is well; for all that befalls you is an ordained part in the weaving of the destiny of all things from the beginning.

Question: How do I forgive myself?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You have endured countless sufferings from not letting your ruling mind do the work it was made for. Enough.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You have already suffered plenty from not letting your better judgement do its job. That is punishment enough. It's like a debt that has been paid in full: you can stop sending money.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You have endured innumerable sufferings by not being satisfied with your own ruling part when it does the things which it was formed to do. Enough then of that.

Question: I keep making the same mistake.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Principles cannot die unless the thoughts that feed them are put out. Kindle them again. It is in your power to live anew.
