If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Your principles fade when the thoughts that feed them go out. Relight them. You can begin again at any point. It's like a campfire that has died down: there are embers under the ash. Add small wood, and blow.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How can the great principles of life become dead if the impressions which correspond to them be not extinguished? These impressions you may still rekindle. I can always form the proper opinion of this or that; and, if so, why am I disturbed?

Question: Should I try something I will probably fail at?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Attempt even what you despair of. The left hand, clumsy for lack of use, holds the reins better than the right, because it has practised.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes. Practise even the things you expect to fail at. The weaker hand grips well where it has been trained. It's like writing with your other hand: hopeless on the first day, and readable after steady practice.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The left hand, which in other things is of little value for want of use, yet holds the bridle more firmly than the right, for in this it has practice.

Question: How do I start over?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look at things again as you once looked at them. In that lies living anew.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look at things again the way you saw them when you were clear. Starting over is mostly a matter of seeing freshly. It's like restarting a frozen computer: nothing new is installed. It comes back up clean.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): See things again as once you saw them, and your life is made new again.

Question: I let down people who relied on me.
Marcus Aurelius would say: People are unjust by omission as well as by act. Put right what can be put right, and do the next thing well.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Not doing what you should have done is a wrong too. Put right what can be put right, and do the next thing well. It's like forgetting to collect a friend from the airport: you call, you apologise, and you get in the car now. Sitting at home feeling awful helps nobody.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Men are often unjust by omissions as well as by actions.

Question: How do I learn from a setback?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The mind converts everything that impedes it into matter for its action. The hindrance becomes help.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The mind can turn whatever blocks it into material. What stood in the way becomes the way forward. It's like a river meeting a rock: it doesn't stop. It finds a new course, and the rock becomes part of the riverbed.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): For the mind can convert and change everything that impedes its activity into matter for its action; hindrance in its work becomes its real help, and every obstruction makes for its progress.

Question: I am embarrassed by a public failure.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Everything is opinion, and opinion rests with you. Remove it, and like a sailor who has rounded the headland you find calm water.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The embarrassment lives in opinion, and your opinion is yours to change. Drop it, and the water is calm. It's like a typo in an email to the whole company: it felt enormous for an afternoon, and by the end of the week nobody remembered it but you.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Reflect that everything is matter of opinion; and opinion rests with yourself, suppress then your opinion, what time you will, and like one who has doubled the cape and reached the bay, you will have calm and stillness everywhere, never a wave.

Question: My business failed. How should I see it?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Did it stop you from being just, generous, sensible and free? Then it has not harmed what is yours, and to bear it nobly is good fortune.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask whether it stopped you from being fair, generous, sensible and free. If not, what is truly yours is intact, and carrying it well is its own good fortune. It's like a chef whose restaurant closes: the building is gone, and everything they know about cooking leaves with them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember, therefore, for the future, upon all occasions of sorrow, to use the maxim: this thing is not misfortune, but to bear it bravely is good fortune.

Question: How do I know when to give up?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If a thing is hard for you, do not conclude that it is beyond human power. If it is possible and proper for a person, count it within your reach.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't mistake "hard for me right now" for "impossible". If people can do it and it is right for a person to do, it is within your reach. It's like a jar lid that won't budge: before deciding it is welded shut, remember that other hands have opened jars like it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If a thing seems to you very difficult to accomplish, conclude not that it is beyond human power. But, if you see that anything is within man's power, and part of his proper work, conclude that you also may attain to it.

Question: How do I deal with guilt?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The wrongdoer wrongs himself. The remedy is also in oneself: stop, and act rightly.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Wrongdoing hurts the one who did it, and the cure is in the same place: stop, and start acting rightly. It's like a splinter: it hurts because it shouldn't be there. Take it out, clean the spot, and let it heal.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The wrong-doer wrongs himself by making himself evil.

Question: How do I stop demanding perfection of myself?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Be content if the smallest thing goes forward.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Be satisfied when even a small thing moves forward. Demanding the perfect result is the surest way to get none. It's like painting a room: one finished wall is a finished wall, even with three still to do.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be satisfied if the smallest thing go well. Consider even such an event as no small matter. For who can change the opinions of men? And without change of opinion what is their state but a slavery, under which they groan, while they pretend to obey?

Question: I have failed at improving myself. What now?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Return to philosophy as one with sore eyes returns to the sponge: for relief, and not for punishment.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Go back to your principles the way you go back to something that soothes: for relief, and never for punishment. It's like returning to the gym after months away: the staff are glad to see you. The only one keeping score of the absence is you.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Love the good to which you return; and come back to Philosophy, not as one who comes to a master, but as one whose eyes ache recurs to sponge and egg, as another has recourse to plasters, or a third to fomentation.

Question: How do I face the consequences of what I did?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Accept what follows as you would a doctor's prescription: bitter, yet ordered toward health.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Take the consequences the way you take a prescription: unpleasant, and part of getting well. It's like a parking ticket: you pay it, you learn where not to park, and it is over.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Yet we obey him gladly in the hope of health. Conceive therefore that, for Nature, the doing of her work and the fulfilling of her purposes are, as it were, her health; and welcome all that happens, even should it seem hard fortune, because it tends to the health of the Universe, and to the prosperity and felicity of Zeus.

Question: What if I never succeed?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Order your life act by act. If each attains its end as far as it can, that suffices. No one can prevent you from that.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Build your life one act at a time. If each act does what it can, that is enough, and no one can prevent it. It's like building a wall: whether or not the cathedral is ever finished, every brick you laid straight is laid straight.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Order your life in its single acts, so that if each, as far as may be, attains its end, it will suffice. In this no one can hinder you.

Question: Is failure shameful?
Marcus Aurelius would say: If the fault is not a wrong of mine, nor a result of it, and the common good is not harmed, why am I troubled by it?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If it wasn't a moral wrong on your part and it didn't hurt the common good, there is nothing to be ashamed of. It's like a scientist whose experiment gives a negative result: nothing dishonourable happened. Something was tried, and something was learned.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If the fault be not my sin, nor a consequence of it, if there be no damage to the common good, why am I perturbed about it? Wherein is the harm to the common good?

Question: How do I stop procrastinating?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Think of your long delay, and of how often the gods gave you a day of grace that you did not use. Your time has a limit set to it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Remember how long you have been putting this off, and how many chances you have already been given. Time is limited. It's like a boarding gate: it stays open for a while, and then it closes whether or not you were ready.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Surely it is high time to understand the Universe of which you are a part, and the Ruler of that Universe, of whom you are an emanation; that a limit is set to your days, which, if you use them not for your enlightenment, will depart, as you yourself will, and return no more.

Question: How do I get out of bed in the morning?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Is it to lie warm under the blankets that I was made?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask yourself whether you were made to stay warm under a duvet. You have work that is yours to do. It's like an alarm clock compared with a reason: the alarm only makes a noise. Knowing what you are getting up for is what gets you out.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Am I equipped for nothing but to lie among the bed-clothes and keep warm? “But,” you say, “it is more pleasant so”. Is pleasure, then, the object of your being, and not action, and the exercise of your powers?

Question: How do I build discipline?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do what falls to your hand with exact dignity, and free yourself from every other thought. You see how few things a person must master to live a quiet and godly life.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Do the task in front of you with care and drop every other thought. You will find that a good life needs very few things mastered. It's like washing one dish properly, and then the next: discipline is built from single, finished acts.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Hourly and earnestly strive, as a Roman and a man, to do what falls to your hand with perfect unaffected dignity, with kindliness, freedom and justice, and free your soul from every other imagination.

Question: How do I change a bad habit?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The mind takes its colour from its most frequent thoughts. Dye it with a steady run of better ones.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Your mind takes on the colour of what you think about most. Change the habit by changing the daily thoughts. It's like a playlist: whatever you play all day is what you end up humming.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The soul takes colour from its impressions, therefore steep it in such thoughts as these:—Wherever a man can live, he can live well. A man can live in a court, therefore he can live well there.

Question: I keep breaking promises to myself.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask to what end you are now using your soul. Whose soul have I at this moment: a child's, a tyrant's, a beast's?
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Check in with yourself: what am I using my mind for right now? Whose mind is this at the moment, a child's, a bully's, an animal's? It's like asking who is driving the car: if a tired child has the wheel, no wonder the promises keep getting broken.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To what end am I using my soul? Let me examine myself as to this on all occasions, and consider what is passing now in that part of me which men call the ruler of the rest.

Question: How can I be consistent?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He whose aim in life is not always one and the same cannot himself be one and the same through life. Fix the aim.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: If your aim keeps changing, you keep changing. Fix one aim and consistency follows. It's like a ship with a fixed destination: the wind shifts daily, and the port stays the same.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He whose aim in life is not always one and the same cannot himself be one and the same through his whole life. But singleness of aim is not sufficient, unless you consider also what that aim ought to be.

Question: What should my morning routine be?
Marcus Aurelius would say: On waking, say: today I shall meet difficult people, and I rise to the work of a human being. Then, as the Pythagoreans advised, look up at the sky.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: On waking, expect difficult people, remember that you are getting up to do a human being's work, and look up at the sky for a moment. It's like checking the weather, the calendar and the view before leaving the house: a minute of orientation shapes the day.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The Pythagoreans recommended that we should look at the heavens in the morning, to put us in mind of beings that go on doing their proper work uniformly and continuously; and of their order, purity and naked simplicity; for there is no veil upon a star.

Question: What should my evening review be?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Ask how you have behaved toward everyone today, and to what end you have been using your soul.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Ask two questions: how did I treat everyone today, and what did I use my mind for? It's like closing the till at the end of the day: a quick, plain count, no drama, and you start tomorrow knowing where you stand.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): To what end am I using my soul? Let me examine myself as to this on all occasions, and consider what is passing now in that part of me which men call the ruler of the rest.

Question: How do I stop being lazy?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not be languid in action, confused in conversation or vague in thought.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Tighten three things: don't be sluggish in what you do, muddled in what you say, or vague in what you think. It's like a blurry photo: usually the fix is small. You hold steady and focus.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Be not languid in action, nor confused in conversation, nor vague in your opinions. Let there be no sudden contractions or forth-sallyings of your soul. In your life be not over-hurried.

Question: How do I stay disciplined without becoming harsh?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He wants the wrestler's firmness with a cheerful face: simplicity, modesty and good humour.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Combine a wrestler's firmness with a cheerful face. Discipline works best with good humour. It's like a personal trainer who makes you laugh: the workout is just as hard, and you actually come back.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Rejoice yourself with simplicity, modesty, and indifference to all things that lie between good and bad. Love mankind, and obey God. “All things,” says someone, “go by law and order.”

Question: How do I keep my principles in mind?
Marcus Aurelius would say: As surgeons keep their instruments always at hand, keep your principles ready.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Keep them ready to hand, as a surgeon keeps instruments laid out. It's like the emergency contacts saved in your phone: you don't want to be searching for them at the moment you need them.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As surgeons have ever their knives and instruments at hand for the sudden emergencies of their art, so do you keep ready the principles requisite for understanding things divine and human, and for doing all things, even the least important, in the remembrance of the bond between the two.

Question: How do I stick with something difficult?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Because a thing is hard for you, do not suppose it beyond human power.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Being hard for you doesn't make it impossible. Others have done it, so it is within human reach, and you are human. It's like the first weeks of learning a language: it sounds like noise, and ordinary people everywhere speak it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If a thing seems to you very difficult to accomplish, conclude not that it is beyond human power. But, if you see that anything is within man's power, and part of his proper work, conclude that you also may attain to it.

Question: How do I stop making excuses?
Marcus Aurelius would say: One man acts the philosopher without a coat, another without books, a third half naked. "I have no bread," says one, "yet I hold to reason."
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People have lived by their principles with no coat, no books and no bread. The conditions are never perfect. It's like waiting for every traffic light on the route to be green before you leave the house.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): One acts the philosopher without a coat, another without books, a third half-naked. Says one, “I have not bread, and yet I hold to reason.” Says another, “I have not even the spiritual food of instruction, and yet I hold to it”.

Question: How long does it take to change?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Within ten days you may seem a god to those who now think you a beast.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Less time than you fear. He says ten days of living by your principles can change how people see you. It's like a neglected garden: a short spell of steady weeding, and it already looks like someone lives there.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Within ten days, if you return to the observance of moral principles and to the cult of reason, you will appear a God to them who now esteem you a wild beast or an ape.

Question: Why can I not do what I know is right?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Discourse no more about what a good man should be. Be one.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Because talking about it has become a substitute for doing it. Stop discussing what a good person is, and be one. It's like reading reviews of running shoes for months: at some point you put on any pair and run.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Discourse no more of what a good man should be; but be one.

Question: How do I practise self-control?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Guard against four turnings of the mind: needless thoughts, thoughts that harm fellowship, speech that is not from the heart, and letting the lower part master the higher.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Watch for four slips: pointless thoughts, thoughts that damage your ties with people, saying what you don't mean, and letting appetite overrule judgement. It's like the warning lights on a dashboard: learn the few that matter, and glance at them often.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): There are four states of the soul against which you must continually and especially be upon your guard; and which, when detected, should be effaced, by remarking thus of each.

Question: What do I do when I relapse?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Return. Do not be disgusted with yourself.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Come back, and don't be disgusted with yourself. It's like falling off a bike: you get back on. Lying next to the bike calling yourself a bad cyclist is not part of the method.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If you are beaten off, return again to the effort, and content yourself that your conduct is generally such as becomes a man. Love the good to which you return; and come back to Philosophy, not as one who comes to a master, but as one whose eyes ache recurs to sponge and egg, as another has recourse to plasters, or a third to fomentation.

Question: Do small daily habits really matter?
Marcus Aurelius would say: A life is ordered in its single acts.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes. A life is made of single acts, arranged one after another. It's like brushing your teeth: no single morning matters much, and the years of mornings are the whole difference.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Order your life in its single acts, so that if each, as far as may be, attains its end, it will suffice. In this no one can hinder you.

Question: How do I keep learning without drowning in information?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Put away the thirst for books, so that you do not die murmuring. Learn for use, and hurry to the goal.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stop hoarding information. Learn what you will use, and get on with living. It's like saving recipe after recipe and never cooking: pick one, and make dinner.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Put from you the thirst of books, that you may not die murmuring, but meekly, and with true and heartfelt gratitude to the Gods.

Question: How do I keep a journal as he did?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Write short, plain notes to yourself and return to them. A few brief principles, revisited, are enough to clear the mind.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Write short, plain notes to yourself and reread them. A few principles revisited do more than pages of new ideas. It's like a note on the fridge door: brief, and seen every day.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Have also at hand thoughts brief and fundamental, which readily may occur; sufficing to shut out the discordant clamour of the world, and to send you back without fretting at the task to which you return.

Question: How do I resist temptation?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Analyse it into its parts. A tune broken into single notes, a dance into single moves, loses its hold. Do this with everything except virtue.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Break the tempting thing into its parts. Taken piece by piece, it loses its pull. It's like a magic trick explained step by step: once you see the mechanics, the spell is gone.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You will think little of a pleasing song, a dance, or a gymnastic display, if you analyse the melody into its separate notes, and ask yourself regarding each, “Does this impress me?”

Question: Is pleasure bad?
Marcus Aurelius would say: How many pleasures have been enjoyed by robbers, tyrants and parricides. Pleasure is no test of what is good.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Pleasure proves nothing by itself. Plenty of terrible people have enjoyed plenty of it, so it can't be the measure of what is good. It's like sweetness: something tasting sweet tells you nothing about whether it feeds you.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How many are the pleasures that have been enjoyed by robbers, rakes, parricides, and tyrants!

Question: How do I cut down on drinking?
Marcus Aurelius would say: This fine wine is the juice of a bunch of grapes. See it so. Like Socrates, be able both to abstain and to enjoy. If stopping is hard, get help.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: See the drink plainly: fermented grape juice. Then aim to be someone who can take it or leave it. It's like a light switch that you control, compared with one that is stuck on. If stopping is hard, get help, as you would with anything else you couldn't shift alone.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): A man might fairly apply that to him which is recorded of Socrates: that he could both abstain from and enjoy these things, in want whereof many show themselves weak, and, in the possession, intemperate.

Question: How do I deal with an addiction?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Let the ruling part be no longer in servitude, dragged like a puppet by every impulse. And take help, as a soldier is helped up a wall. This needs more than a principle.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: The part of you that decides shouldn't be dragged around by every impulse. And take help, the way a soldier takes a hand up a wall. It's like a car stuck in mud: more revving digs it deeper. You need a tow, and calling for one is the smart move. This needs more than a principle.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As to this, take heed, now that you are old, that it remain no longer in servitude; that it be no more dragged hither and thither like a puppet by every selfish impulse. Repine no more at what fate now sends, nor dread what may befall you hereafter.

Question: Why do I want things that are bad for me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Desire pulls like a puppet's string. The thing that works the strings is hidden within, and it can be watched.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A want pulls like a string, and the hand on the string is inside you, where it can be watched. It's like advertising: once you notice how the advert is built to make you want, you start wanting less.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Remember that the mover of the puppet strings is the hidden principle within. It is that which is eloquence; that which is life; that, if I may say so, which is the man. Never, in your imagination, confound that principle with the surrounding earthen vessel and the little organs that are kneaded on to it.

Question: How do I stop overindulging?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Nature has set limits to eating and drinking, as it has to rest. Do not go past what is sufficient.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Nature sets a limit: enough food, enough drink, enough rest. Trouble starts past "enough". It's like filling a glass: the water is good right up to the rim, and after that it is a mess on the table.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Assuredly; but nature appoints a measure for rest, just as for eating and drinking. In rest you go beyond these limits, and beyond what is enough; but in action you do not fill the measure, and remain well within your powers.

Question: How do I enjoy things without excess?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Use what fortune gives without pride, and do not crave it when it is missing.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Enjoy what comes your way without pride, and don't crave it when it is missing. It's like good weather: you enjoy the sunny day fully, and you don't spend the cloudy one in mourning.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): As to the things which make the ease of life, and which fortune can supply in such abundance, he used them without pride, and yet with all freedom: enjoyed them without affectation when they were present, and when absent he found no want of them.

Question: How do I break the pull of my phone, gambling or other compulsions?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Wipe out the impression, stay the impulse, quench the desire. Then give the freed attention to the work of the moment. If it has become a real compulsion, get help.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Cut the picture, hold the urge, cool the want, and put the freed attention on what you are doing. It's like moving an app off your home screen: one extra step between the urge and the tap is often all it takes. If it has become a real compulsion, get help.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Wipe out impression; stay impulse; quench desire; and keep the governing part master of itself.

Question: Is it wrong to want luxury?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He finds no virtue set against justice. He does find one set against the love of pleasure: self-control.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He notes that there is a virtue whose whole job is to check the love of pleasure: self-control. Wanting is no crime, and it needs a governor. It's like the brakes on a fast car: they are what makes the speed safe to enjoy.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In the constitution of the rational being I discern no virtue made to restrain justice; but I see continence made to restrain sensual pleasure.

Question: How do I stop wanting what other people have?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do not dwell on what you lack as though it were already yours. Dwell on what you have.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stop daydreaming about what you lack, and look at what you already hold. It's like the grass on the other side of the fence: it looks greener from a distance, and your own improves when you water it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Dwell not on what you lack so much as on what you have already. Select the best of what you have, and consider how passionately you would have longed for it had it not been yours.

Question: How do I deal with lust or pornography?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He strips the act of its glamour, describing it as plainly as he describes food and wine. See the thing itself.

Question: How do I live in the present?

Question: How do I stop being scattered?

Marcus Aurelius would say: What happens to each of us is ordered and fitted to us, as a doctor fits the treatment to the patient.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: What happens to each of us fits into a larger order, the way a doctor matches a treatment to a patient. It's like a coach's training plan: single sessions can seem pointless or harsh, and the season shows what they were for.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): in the first case, means that such treatment was enjoined on the patient as might coincide with the needs of his health: in the second case it means that each man's fortune is appointed to coincide with the purposes of fate.

Question: What should I do when I do not know what to do?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Do justice with all your heart, and speak the truth. For the rest, do the duty in front of you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: When you don't know, fall back on the basics: act fairly, tell the truth, and do the task in front of you. It's like being lost on a walk: you stop, find the nearest path you can trust, and follow it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The safety of life is to see the whole nature of everything, and to discern the matter and the form of its constitution; also to do justice with all your heart, and to speak the truth.

Question: What is the purpose of life?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Everything is formed for some work: the horse, the vine. A human being is formed to be kindly to others and to use reason well.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Everything is built for a job. A human being is built to be good to others and to think well. It's like a key: it can be used as a paperweight, and it is only doing what it was made for when it opens a door.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The horse, the vine—all things are formed for some purpose. Where is the wonder? Even the sun saith, “I was formed for a certain work”; and similarly the other Gods. For what end are you formed?

Question: How do I find meaning?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Life is short, and its one fruit in this world is a pure mind and unselfish conduct.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Meaning doesn't have to be found far away. In a short life, the real harvest is a clear mind and conduct that serves others. It's like a fruit tree: it doesn't go searching for its purpose. It bears fruit.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Life is short, and the one fruit of it in this world is a pure mind and unselfish conduct. Be in all things the disciple of Antonine. Imitate his resolute constancy to rational action, his level equability, his godliness, his serenity of countenance, his sweetness of temper, his contempt of vainglory, his keen attempts to comprehend things.

Question: Does my life matter in such a vast universe?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You are a part of the whole. Small as the part is, what serves the whole serves you, and you have your work in it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You are a part of the whole, and the whole needs its parts. Small is not the same as pointless. It's like a single bolt in an aircraft wing: tiny, and nobody would fly without it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whether all be atoms, or there be a universal Law of Nature, let it be laid down first that I am a part of the whole which is governed by Nature; secondly, that I am associated with other parts like myself.

Question: Did Marcus believe in God?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He speaks of the gods and of universal reason with reverence, and argues from their effects: I have not seen my own soul either, yet I honour it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He speaks of the gods and of a universal reason with reverence, and argues from effects: you have never seen your own mind either, and you don't doubt it. It's like the wind: nobody has seen it, and nobody doubts what is moving the trees.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Again, my own soul I cannot see, and yet I reverence it. Thus, too, as regards the Gods, I continually feel their power; and so I know that they exist, and I worship them.

Question: What if there is no God, only chance?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Even then, be glad to have a ruling mind of your own. If all else is random, do not be random yourself.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Even then, be glad you have a mind that can govern itself. If the world is random, that is no reason for you to be. It's like a small boat on a rough sea: the waves are chaos, and the hand on the tiller isn't.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Either the Universal Mind exerts itself in every particular event, in which case you must accept what comes immediately from it: or it has exerted itself once and for all, and, as a result, all things go on for ever, in a necessary chain of consequence: or again atoms and indivisible particles are the origin of all things.

Question: How should I pray?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Simply and freely, as the Athenians prayed for rain. And pray for the inner thing: not to fear, not to crave.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Simply and freely. And ask for the inner thing: not "give me this", but "help me not to fear, and not to crave". It's like asking for a stronger back, where you used to ask for a lighter load.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): This is a prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, on the plains and ploughlands of the Athenians.” Man should either not pray at all, or pray after this frank and simple fashion.

Question: Why do bad things happen to good people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Death and life, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty befall good and bad alike. So they are neither good nor evil in themselves.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Because health, wealth, pain and loss land on good and bad people alike. That shows they are neither rewards nor punishments, and so not the true good or bad. It's like a lottery: the winning ticket tells you nothing about the character of the winner.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Now death and life, glory and reproach, pain and pleasure, riches and poverty—all these happen equally to the good and to the bad. But, as they are neither honourable nor shameful, they are therefore neither good nor evil.

Question: Is everything fated?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Whatever happens was prepared from all eternity. Yet no one can rob you of your freedom to judge and to act.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Events arrive through a long chain of causes. Your judgement and your response are still yours, and no one can take them. It's like weather and clothing: you don't choose the forecast, and you do choose what to wear.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Whatever happens to you was prearranged for you from all eternity; and the concatenation of causes had from eternity interwoven your existence with this contingency.

Question: What is my duty?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Each hour, to do what falls to your hand with dignity, kindness, freedom and justice.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Hour by hour, to do what is in front of you with dignity, kindness, freedom and fairness. It's like a shift at work: you don't have to plan the whole career today. You do this shift well.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Hourly and earnestly strive, as a Roman and a man, to do what falls to your hand with perfect unaffected dignity, with kindliness, freedom and justice, and free your soul from every other imagination.

Question: What does it mean to live according to nature?
Marcus Aurelius would say: For a reasoning being, to act according to nature is to act according to reason.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: For a thinking creature, living by nature means living by reason. It's like using a tool for what it was designed to do: a pair of scissors lives according to its nature when it cuts well.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): In the reasoning being to act according to nature is to act according to reason.

Question: What am I, really?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Body, breath and mind. The first two are yours only to care for. The third alone is truly your own.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Body, breath and mind. The first two you only look after. The third is the part that is really you. It's like a driver in a hire car: you take care of the car, and you are not the car.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Of these the two first are yours in so far as they must have your care; the third only is properly your own.

Question: Why are we here together?
Marcus Aurelius would say: People were created for one another.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Because people are made for each other. Nobody is built to be complete alone, and what one person lacks another supplies. It's like the pieces of a jigsaw: each one is cut with gaps and tabs because it was meant to join the others.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Men were created the one for the other. Teach them better then, or bear with them.

Question: I feel spiritually empty.
Marcus Aurelius would say: Live with the gods: show them a soul content with its lot and doing what the spirit within directs.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stay close to what is highest: show it a mind content with its lot and doing what your better self directs. It's like a daily walk with someone you respect: the regular company changes you more than any single conversation.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): And he lives with the Gods who continually displays to them his soul, living in satisfaction with its lot, and doing the will of the inward spirit, a portion of his own divinity which Zeus has given to every man for a ruler and a guide.

Question: How do I see wonder in the world?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Watch the stars in their courses as though you were running alongside them.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Follow the stars across the sky as if you were travelling with them. Wonder is a matter of attention. It's like lying on your back in a field far from city lights: the sky was there all along. You just hadn't looked up.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Contemplate the courses of the stars, as one should do that revolves along with them. Consider also without ceasing the changes of elements, one into another. Speculations upon such things cleanse away the filth of this earthly life.

Question: Is the universe on my side?
Marcus Aurelius would say: The universe loves to bring about whatever is coming to be. Say to it, then: I love as you love.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Nature is always bringing things into being, and you can choose to love what it brings. Say to it: I love what you love. It's like dancing with a partner who leads: it goes far better when you move with the music.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The Universe loves to bring about whatever is coming to be. I then will say to the Universe: “What thou lovest I love.” Is it not a common saying that, “so-and-so loves to happen”?

Question: What can philosophy do for me?
Marcus Aurelius would say: It alone can guide: keeping the spirit within free from harm, above pain and pleasure, doing nothing aimlessly or falsely.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: It gives you a guide: keep your inner self unharmed, above pleasure and pain, doing nothing pointlessly or falsely. It's like the keel of a boat: invisible below the waterline, and the reason the boat stays upright.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): And this consists in keeping the divinity within inviolate and intact; victorious over pain and pleasure; free from temerity, free from falsehood, free from hypocrisy; independent of what others do or fail to do; submissive to hap and lot, which come from the same source as we; and, above all, with equanimity awaiting death, as nothing else than a resolution of the elements of which every being compounded.

Question: Where do I find guidance within?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Look inward. Within is the spring of good, and it will flow if you keep digging.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Look inward. The source of good is there, and it keeps flowing as long as you keep digging. It's like a compass you already carry: you don't need to buy one. You need to take it out and look at it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Look inward. Within is the fountain of Good. Dig constantly and it will ever well forth.

Question: What should I revere?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Revere the best thing in the universe, and likewise the best thing in yourself. They are of one kind.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Honour the best thing in the universe, and the best thing in yourself, your reason, which is of the same kind. It's like a spark and the sun: different in size, and the same fire.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Reverence that which is most excellent in the Universe, and the most excellent is that which employs all things and rules all. Likewise reverence that which is most excellent in yourself.

Question: Am I part of something larger?
Marcus Aurelius would say: All things are twined together in one sacred bond. Scarcely one thing is foreign to another.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Yes. Everything is tied to everything else, and almost nothing stands alone. It's like the internet: your device looks separate, and it only works because it is linked to all the others.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): All things are twined together, in one sacred bond. Scarce is there one thing quite foreign to another. They are all ranged together, and leagued to form the same ordered whole.

Question: What makes a life complete?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Five acts or three, the play is complete when the one who composed it lets the actor go.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Completeness is not about length. The play is complete when its author says so, whether it had five acts or three. It's like a short story: it is no unfinished novel. It is whole at the length it was written.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): say you, “I have not spoken my five acts, but only three.” True, but in life three acts make up the play. For he sets the end who was responsible for its composition at the first, and for its present dissolution.

Question: How can I be a good person?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Discuss it no longer. Be one.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Stop debating it and start. You already know roughly what a good person does. The gap is in the doing. It's like learning to swim: no amount of reading at the poolside gets you wet.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Discourse no more of what a good man should be; but be one.

Question: Why be honest?
Marcus Aurelius would say: A lie is a wrong against the nature of the whole, which is truth. Even the one who lies unwillingly is out of tune with it.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: A lie works against the way things are, and reality is built on truth. Even a careless untruth puts you out of step with it. It's like one wrong number in a spreadsheet: every total that depends on it is now off.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): He, then, that lies willingly is guilty of impiety, in so far as by deceiving he works injury: and he also who lies unwillingly, in so far as he is out of tune with universal Nature, and in so far as he works disorder in the Universe by fighting against its design.

Question: How honest should I be?
Marcus Aurelius would say: How rotten is the one who says "I mean to deal straightforwardly with you". Sincerity needs no announcement. It shows at once in the face.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Completely, and without announcing it. Real sincerity doesn't need a preface. It shows straight away. It's like a clean restaurant: it doesn't need a sign saying "we are clean". You can see it when you walk in.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How rotten and insincere is his profession who says, “I mean to deal straightforwardly with you.” What are you doing, man? There is no need for such a preface. It will appear of itself.

Question: What are the main virtues?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Justice, truth, self-control and courage.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: There are four: being fair to people, telling the truth, governing your own wants, and doing the right thing when it is frightening. Everything else he praises is a version of these. It's like the four legs of a table: take one away, and nothing you put on it is safe.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If in the life of man you find anything better than justice, truth, sobriety, manliness; and, in sum, anything better than the satisfaction of your soul with itself in that wherein it is given to you to follow right reason; and with fate in that which is determined beyond your control; if, I say, you find aught better than this, then turn thereto with all your heart, and enjoy it as the best that is to be found.

Question: How can I be kind when I do not feel like it?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Kindness is the proper work of a human being. When you do it, you have done what you were made for, and that is the reward.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Kindness is the work you were made for, so doing it is its own reward, with or without the feeling. It's like going for a run on a day you don't fancy it: you do it anyway, and the good feeling shows up afterwards.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): What would you more, when you have done a man a kindness? Is it not enough for you that you have acted in this according to your nature? Do you ask a reward for it? It is as if the eye were to ask a reward for seeing, or the feet for walking.

Question: Why should I help others?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Have I done something for the common good? Then I have my advantage. What does not profit the swarm does not profit the bee.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Because what helps the group helps you. You are part of it. It's like bailing water out of a shared boat: nobody asks whose side of the boat the leak is on.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Have I done anything for the common good? Is not this itself my advantage? Let this thought be ever with you, and desist not.

Question: Does kindness make me a pushover?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Meekness is invincible if it is genuine, and not a simper or an act. Gentleness, and not anger, is the manly thing.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: No. Real gentleness, not the fake smiling kind, can't be beaten, and it takes more strength than anger. It's like a tall building designed to sway a little in the wind: the give is part of the strength.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Ninthly: Meekness is invincible if it be genuine, without simper or hypocrisy. For what can the most insolent of men do to you, if you persist in civility towards him; and, if occasion offers, admonish him gently and deliberately, shew him the better way at the very moment that he is endeavouring to harm you?

Question: How do I do good without wanting credit?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Like a horse that has run, a hound that has tracked, a bee that has made honey.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Do the good and go on to the next thing, the way a horse runs or a bee makes honey. It's like a street cleaner at dawn: the street is clean when the city wakes, and nobody saw who did it.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): The horse when he has run his course, the hound when he has followed the track, the bee when it has made its honey, and the man when he has done good to others, make no noisy boast of it, but set out to do the same once more, as the vine in its season produces its new clusters again.

Question: How do I keep my integrity when no one is watching?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Never value anything that makes you want what needs walls and curtains.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Want nothing that needs walls and curtains to hide it. It's like a house with the lights on and the blinds up: nothing going on inside needs the blinds down.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Never esteem aught of advantage which will oblige you to break your faith, or to desert your honour; to hate, to suspect, or to execrate any man; to play a part; or to set your mind on anything that needs to be hidden by wall or curtain.

Question: How can I be more patient with ignorant people?
Marcus Aurelius would say: No soul parts willingly with the truth. Remembering this makes one gentler toward everyone.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Nobody gives up the truth on purpose. People are wrong because they don't see it. Remember that, and you will be gentler. It's like someone driving with a dirty windscreen: they aren't steering badly for fun. They can't see the road.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): says Plato, “parts unwillingly with truth.” You may say the same of justice, temperance, good-nature, and every virtue. It is most necessary to keep this ever in mind; for, if you do, you will be more kindly towards all men.

Question: Is it all right to lie in order to be kind?
Marcus Aurelius would say: He allows no exception: if it is not true, do not say it. He would have the truth told with tact.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: He allows no exception: if it isn't true, don't say it. But tell the truth with tact. It's like a doctor with difficult news: the facts stay the same, and the choice of words and timing is where the kindness lives.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): If a thing be not becoming, do it not; if not true, say it not.

Question: How should I treat strangers?
Marcus Aurelius would say: As fellow citizens. If reason is common to us all, so is law, and the world is like one city.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: As fellow citizens of one city. If we all share reason, we share a law and a community. It's like passengers on the same train: different seats and different tickets, and one journey.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Therefore we have all a common law; and if so, we are fellow-citizens and members of some common polity. The Universe, then, must in a manner be a state, for of what other common polity can all mankind be said to be members?

Question: How should I treat animals and the natural world?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Use animals and material things in a spirit of generosity and freedom, as one who has reason toward those who have none.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Generously and freely, as the one who can reason dealing with those who can't. It's like being the adult in a room of small children: the power you hold over them is exactly why you have to be gentle.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Use the brute creation, and also all material things, in the spirit of magnanimity and freedom which becomes him who has reason in using that which has it not. Towards men, who have reason, act in a social spirit.

Question: What do I owe society?
Marcus Aurelius would say: You are a part that completes a social system. Let every act of yours complete a social life.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: You are a part that completes a community, so let each thing you do contribute to it. It's like a shared dinner where everyone brings a dish: it only works if everyone brings one.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): You yourself are a part of a social system necessary to complete the whole. Accordingly, let your every action be a similar part of the social life. And if any action has not its reference, either immediate or distant, to the common good as its end, this action disorders your life and frustrates its unity.

Question: What is justice?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Nature formed reasoning beings for one another, to help each according to desert and never to harm. To act against this is injustice.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: People are made for one another, to help according to need and merit, and never to harm. Injustice is acting against that. It's like the rules of the road: traffic works because each driver gives the others what they are due.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): For since universal Nature has formed the rational animals for one another; each to be useful to the other according to his merit, and never hurtful; he who transgresses this her will is clearly guilty of impiety against the most ancient and venerable of the Gods.

Question: How can I be humble?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Like Antoninus, have no love of empty fame. And recall how small a part of the ages is allotted to you.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Don't chase empty fame, and remember how small a slice of time is yours. It's like one frame in a very long film: needed by the film, and no reason to think the film is about you.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): How small a part of the boundless immensity of the ages is allotted to each of us, and presently that will vanish in eternity! How little is ours of the universal substance; how little of the universal spirit!

Question: How do I keep my word?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Count nothing an advantage that obliges you to break your faith.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Count nothing as a gain if it makes you break your word. It's like a signature: once people learn that it can't be trusted, it is worth nothing on any document.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Never esteem aught of advantage which will oblige you to break your faith, or to desert your honour; to hate, to suspect, or to execrate any man; to play a part; or to set your mind on anything that needs to be hidden by wall or curtain.

Question: How can I be cheerful and good-natured?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Keep a cheerful mind that needs no help from outside, and no peace that depends on others.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Keep a cheerfulness that doesn't depend on outside help or on other people behaving well. It's like a house with its own solar panels: the lights stay on when the grid goes down.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): And withal, be cheerful, and independent of the assistance and the peace that comes from others; for, it is a man's duty to stand upright, self-supporting, not supported.

Question: How do I live simply and sincerely?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Guard your simplicity, your goodness, your sincerity and your dignity.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Guard four things: keeping life simple, being good to people, meaning what you say, and carrying yourself with self-respect. Most complications begin when one of them is dropped. It's like plain window glass: nothing added, nothing hidden, and it does its job perfectly.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Guard your simplicity, your goodness, your sincerity, your dignity, your reticence, your love of justice, your piety, your kindliness, your affection for your kin, and your constancy to your duty.

Question: What does a good life come down to?
Marcus Aurelius would say: Life is short. Its one fruit is a pure mind and unselfish conduct.
If he grew up today (plain words, then a: Life is short, and what it yields is a clear mind and actions that serve others. Everything else is packaging. It's like an orange: what you were after is the fruit, and not the peel.
Passage (Chrystal translation, 1902): Life is short, and the one fruit of it in this world is a pure mind and unselfish conduct. Be in all things the disciple of Antonine. Imitate his resolute constancy to rational action, his level equability, his godliness, his serenity of countenance, his sweetness of temper, his contempt of vainglory, his keen attempts to comprehend things.
